#5671. Hummer H1s May Be Nearly Indestructible, But Some Serious Flaws Live In That 'Nearly' Part

The Hummer brand officially launched in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model. Much like the popularity of the Willys Jeep in post-WWII America, the H1 capitalized on rah-rah post-Gulf War nationalism and a personal endorsement from Arnold Schwarzenegger to find its place in the automotive zeitgeist. After being awarded its first military production contract in 1983, the big diesel-powered machine was well-proven by the time John Q. Public could place an order a decade later. If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no.

When it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the new millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

Because of its high profile and rarity, every variant of the H1 generally still commands a pretty penny, even two decades after production ended. A high-mileage early non-turbo diesel model might bring as low as $35,000, while a low-mileage 2006-only H1 Alpha runs into the low six-figure range. If you're going to be spending that much money to get yourself one of these rolling monuments of gender-affirming care, what trouble should you expect and look out for? Let's dig into it.

The first issue is that, simply due to their size and material density, they're really heavy. At around 7,500 pounds, you're moving a lot of metal around. Weight translates to atrocious fuel economy, like about 10 miles per gallon bad. Another downside: due to the military-based nature of these trucks, driver comfort is hardly a concern, and the noise, vibration, and harshness engineers were not really consulted in the design phase. According to a Hagerty review, the "engine sounds like a jackhammer inside the cockpit." Oh, and it doesn't have airbags.

On the plus side, a Hummer H1 is mostly indestructible, except for one major flaw. If you're a long-time reader of Jalopnik, you'll probably know where this is going, because over a decade ago our own Doug Demuro found out firsthand what breaks on the Hummer H1. I'll let him explain it.

"Beginning in about 1996, every single Hummer was fitted with a 6.5-liter Detroit Diesel turbodiesel V8, which combined the 194 horsepower of a Toyota Camry with the 438 lb-ft of torque from an angry farm tractor.

Well, there was one little issue: every single one of these engines was manufactured with a casting flaw that resulted in a crack on the number eight cylinder. Fortunately, the fix was easy: you just replaced the engine.

But check this out: it affected every single Hummer manufactured from 1996 to 2000... Every single Hummer built from 1996 to 2000 has either had its engine fail due to the number eight cylinder issue, or will have its engine fail."

The pre-1996 non-turbo Detroit Diesel-powered models, the rare gasoline-powered model, and the 2001-2006 models are unaffected. Check the engine casting number and make sure it was made after March 15, 1999.

There is another major issue with Hummer H1 trucks, but it's significantly less catastrophic than a failed engine. The onboard tire inflation-deflation system leaks because, of course, it does. Especially after a couple of decades of sitting on display with low-mileage odometers, the rubber lines of the system tend to crack and drop pressure. It's possible to replace all of the lines and make it function again, and there are ways to bypass the system altogether and inflate your tires the old-fashioned way.

There are plenty of other issues that come with buying a twenty-year-old truck. Just like anything with decades of wear, keep an eye on worn suspension components, leaks, rust, ill-maintained brakes, and maintenance records. According to TireRack.com, a set of H1 tires will cost up to $2,240, so that information might help you negotiate. Also, because this is a rare machine, you probably won't find any of the parts you need for things like the tire inflation system at your local corner parts store. The parts exist, but you might want to keep the Hummer Parts Guy on speed dial.

There are plenty of options for '96 to 2000 trucks that haven't had their engines replaced yet. If you can get one for cheap, it might make the basis of an interesting project truck. I'm imagining a rare two-door pickup H1s with a Duramax "Mongoose" 8.3-liter turbo diesel V8, the one found in the current Chevrolet and GMC HD trucks making 555 horsepower and 1,230 lb-ft of torque. That might be the only way to make an actually fast Hummer.

2026 has been a year of significant robotaxi news. One might say it’s been the year of the robotaxi. “The autonomous vehicle industry has made remarkable strides this year, bringing us closer to a future of safer, more accessible mobility. With the launch of our fully driverless ride-hailing service using a purposefully designed robotaxi, we’re thrilled to be part of this groundbreaking journey,” adds Aicha Evans, CEO of Zoox. “Las Vegas is a city famous for unforgettable moments, and it is the ideal location for our debut. Zoox is about transforming the entire ride-hailing experience, making every ride a delightful experience.”

#5669. The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.

On November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective new metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering.

The winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.

In my new TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction, I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining company needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful new evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Company uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

The history of first-of-a-kind offshore production should influence the financing. Nautilus Minerals spent substantial capital on its Solwara-1 venture without reaching commercial production. Deep-sea mining depends on specialized machines, ships, handling systems, processing capacity and sales contracts working in sequence. The first production years of comparable projects are rarely smooth. The lease is one of the cheapest and earliest commitments in that chain.

American Samoa also has its own decision to make. Its government has supported scientific investigation while withholding support for commercial extraction at present. A lawsuit filed by Samoan chiefs and community groups contests the federal process. The resulting legal and territorial questions matter alongside engineering and economics. The environmental finding for preliminary leasing activities is not a finding about the effects of a future commercial mine.

Auction results will show what qualified bidders will pay for an opportunity. A winning bid can justify a company’s further studies and improve its fundraising story. An operating business will require years of capital investment, production evidence and profitable metal sales. Those are much harder milestones, and they remain ahead of the bidders.

Read A Seabed Lease Does Not Fix a Broken Business Case for the full assessment of the auction, and the Barnard–Trytten report for the underlying engineering and financial analysis.

#5668. The Test Bed For Jaguar's XJ220 Twin-Turbo V6 Was A Ford Transit Van

Jaguar is in a strange place right now because it's wedged between two very different versions of itself. In front lies a future defined by a bold design language and electric powertrains, ushered in by perhaps the most divisive car in a generation: the 1,015-hp, 400-mile 2028 Type 01 sedan. Behind it is a century-old story about craftsmanship, passion, and a great big dollop of supercharger whine. There was the absolutely stunning E-Type, which Enzo Ferrari famously christened as the most beautiful car in the world, and let's not forget the bonkers V12-powered XJR-9 that not only won Le Mans, but was voted as one of your favorite sports prototype race cars of all time.

Then there's the XJ220 — arguably the most curious chapter of them all. It had a difficult start to life because Jaguar opted for a last-minute switch from a V12 to a twin-turbo V6 and from all-wheel drive to rear-wheel drive, instantly making it less sexy and appealing to customers than rivals like the Bugatti EB110 and Ferrari F40. Instead, the XJ220 did its talking with sheer force, clocking a 217-mph top speed to become the world's fastest production car in 1992. Imagine how smug its engineers felt.

What's interesting about its twin-turbo V6 is how it was tested. We all know manufacturers use test mule cars to iron out any pre-production issues, but these normally have some sort of resemblance to the final car. For the XJ220, Jaguar and its development partner Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR) decided to use a humble Ford Transit. Yes, a Ford Transit. If you're thinking this sounds familiar, it's because it was the same vehicle Richard Hammond used in a drag race against a Holden Maloo truck, when the original "Top Gear" trio competed against their Aussie counterparts.

Most likely, discretion. The XJ220 was a tight-lipped secret around the Jaguar offices, and when TWR had finalized the engine setup and wanted to run its various litmus tests, it had to do so very carefully. So, what better to use to disguise your shiny new, world-record-chasing motor than something absolutely nobody would suspect?

Based on a 1989 long-wheelbase Ford Transit, the exterior looked almost identical to a slightly worn example, with the only potential giveaway being the ZR performance tires and identical alloy wheels to those that would eventually end up on the XJ220. But if you were to open up the cargo bed, you'd spot the 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 — originally rated at 540 horsepower — and suspiciously racy running gear lurking low down.

An interesting fact is that this engine is actually closely related to the engine in the MG 6R4 — a monstrous rally car, and arguably the only cool car MG has ever built. You see, the 6R4 was built for Group B, which ended in 1986, and thus meant MG had no use for a properly decked-out six-cylinder engine anymore. It then reportedly sold the rights and design infrastructure to TWR, and that's how it eventually wound up in the XJ220.

If you thought it was heading for a peaceful retirement in the Scottish Highlands, you'd be dead wrong. Once TWR had finished work with it, the Transit was acquired by the Benetton Formula 1 team, which used it as a parts delivery vehicle. It might have been on the verge of being scrapped after Benetton was done with it, but then, in stepped a savior: Don Law Racing.

Don Law Racing is widely considered to be the world's leading XJ220 specialist. The rightful heir to the Frankenstein Transit project, then. The company worked on the vehicle and got it back up to condition, and once it eventually did, it appeared in places like the Goodwood Festival of Speed, where it has indeed been up the hill on multiple occasions and left unsuspecting spectators in awe. Quite the fairy-tale ending, wouldn't you say?

You've likely seen those neat little mini trucks from Japan. They're the size of a compact vehicle, but have a bed as long as some full-size pickups. These Kei trucks, as they are called, look like they would be pretty practical for a number of uses.

President Trump was quite smitten with Kei trucks when he saw them in Japan, apparently for the first time, later calling them "really cute." And in a December 2025 Truth Social post, he said that he had "approved" the manufacture of these "tiny" vehicles here. But, as is the case with many of the president's statements, no one is quite sure what that means. Unfortunately, you can't buy a new one for road use in the U.S., but older ones are available thanks to an exception in import laws.

Maybe you're thinking about snagging one of these trucks for your farm, ranch, or construction site and wondering how they compare to those side-by-sides that are made for work. These utility task vehicles (UTVs) also have a bed on the back and are often used to haul small loads around on a worksite. There are several differences. For one thing, you can easily find new UTVs for sale. Their payload and towing capacities are often higher than those of most Kei trucks. They are built more for off-roading, while Kei trucks are built for the street. It really comes down to what your needs are, though.

Kei trucks were not made to meet U.S. safety and environmental standards. The Clean Air Act prohibits importing a vehicle that doesn't meet federal emissions standards unless it's at least 21 years old. Federal law also bans foreign vehicles less than 25 years old that don't meet safety standards.

Newer Kei trucks can be imported only as off-road vehicles, permanently limited to 25 mph. That means if you want one for the road, you're stuck shopping for used Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old. That's not to say they're hard to find. Type "used Kei truck for sale" into Google and you'll see several listings for Kei trucks, as well as businesses that sell them. And the ones we've seen look to be in better shape than the typical 25- or 30-year-old vehicle, on the outside at least.

It's a bit more straightforward with UTVs, or side-by-sides. They are off-road vehicles, so they are perfectly legal to sell brand-new in the U.S. We found 25 Polaris dealerships and at least 30 Honda Powersports dealerships in the state of Florida alone. Of course, there are plenty of used side-by-sides all over the place, as well. Sites like ATV Trader, ATVHunt, and Autotrader all contain several listings.

You're going to get a longer, more versatile bed with a mini truck than you will with a UTV. Anyone can see that just by looking at the two vehicles. Kei truck beds are often over 6 feet long and over 4 feet wide. With the tailgate down, that's big enough to haul a piece of plywood or drywall, with just a little bit hanging over the edge.

The sides of a Kei truck's bed often fold down, allowing for easy loading of a packed pallet by a forklift. The walls are not very high, which makes it easier to load and offload the bed, as well. Beds on UTVs are often much smaller, with the boxes on some models being around 3.5 feet in length and a little over 4 feet in width.

Don't confuse bed size with payload capacity, however. Kei trucks, as regulated by the Japanese government, can carry no more than 771 pounds of cargo. On the other hand, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 has a box capacity of 1,500 pounds, which is on the high end for UTVs. We should point out, though, that payload capacity is the final word on how much you can load into your vehicle. The total weight of passengers in the cab and cargo in the box should not exceed payload capacity, regardless of box capacity.

Comparing the towing capacities of mini trucks and side-by-sides is tricky because there aren't any official towing capacities published for Kei trucks. Japan's registration calculation caps the total weight of a brakeless trailer at half of the truck's curb weight. That puts the limit for an unbraked trailer at around 700 to 800 pounds for an older Kei truck, including the trailer.

That's as close as you can get without a written capacity from the manufacturer. You will find people online who insist they can tow more with their Kei truck, but just because some random person claims to have regularly towed over 1,000 pounds without wrecking their Kei truck doesn't mean that you should try it with yours. Nor should you go by the rated capacity of an aftermarket tow hitch. That is the rating of the tow hitch, not of your vehicle. Overall, it's best to stick to light towing when it comes to Kei trucks.

On the other hand, the towing capacities of UTVs are typically straightforward. You'll find the capacities listed in their specs, and those specs vary from model to model. For example, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 NorthStar is rated to tow 3,500 pounds, while the Honda Pioneer 520 is rated to tow 1,000 pounds. If your towing needs involve heavy loads, UTVs are probably the way to go.

You can use either type of vehicle off-road. This is where side-by-sides shine, though, as they were designed specifically for handling rough terrain. Let's start with the tires. You can see from pictures of Kei trucks that they usually come fitted with small street tires that look like they belong on a compact car. UTV tires, on the other hand, often look like tractor tires or tires that go on an ATV. They are made to kick up mud and to laugh at messy terrain.

Clearance is another difference between mini trucks and side-by-sides. The Suzuki Carry mini truck has a ground clearance of around 6 inches. However, the ground clearance for the Honda Pioneer 520 side-by-side is 8.7 inches. The ground clearance for the Polaris Ranger XP 1000 is 14 inches. Of course, the drivetrain is also important when it comes to handling off-road terrain. It's not hard to find a used Kei truck with 4WD. UTVs are typically equipped with AWD, and some can switch between multiple drive modes.

While UTVs excel at off-road performance, we can't say that Kei trucks have to stick to the street. The inclusion of 4WD allows them to hold their own. They are well suited for hard-packed soil, gravel roads, some construction sites, and level ground. But if you have really rough, uneven ground, deep muddy ruts, large rocks, and other obstacles to deal with, our money is on the UTVs.

It probably seems obvious that mini trucks would hold the advantage when it comes to street legality. After all, Kei trucks were made for streets, while side-by-sides were made for off-roading. It's not that simple, though. Sure, the federal government allows Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old to be imported, but that doesn't mean they are road-legal in your state.

Colorado, for example, does not currently allow Kei vehicles to be registered or titled, but that changes on January 1, 2028. After that, Kei vehicles will be allowed on Colorado roads that have a speed limit of 55 miles per hour or less. Pennsylvania allows mini trucks to be registered only with an off-road title, with a farm exemption, or with an antique registration, unless the owner holds a grandfathered registration from 2021. Imported Kei vehicles at least 25 years old are now fully road-legal in Alaska.

Side-by-sides are actually street-legal in certain states. Arizona will issue a motorcycle-style plate to UTVs that have been specifically modified for street use. South Dakota has a similar law. In Colorado, counties and towns decide whether side-by-sides can use their roads, and some towns allow them only during certain hours. Trails are a different matter. The controlling authority for each patch of land that has trails determines which kinds of vehicles are allowed on them. The bottom line is to check the laws of your locality before deciding which vehicle to purchase.

In all of the excitement of finding a mini truck or buying a new side-by-side, it's easy to forget to think about the cost and time that need to go into maintaining these vehicles. Fortunately, maintenance isn't that hard for either type of vehicle. There are some things you want to consider, however.

The recommended frequency of maintenance for side-by-sides is similar to that of motorcycles. Polaris, for example, recommends that the first service for a new Ranger 1000 happen around the 25-hour or 500-mile mark and that the oil and filter then be changed every 200 hours, 2,000 miles, or year, whichever comes first. It's recommended to service the vehicle twice as frequently if it's been exposed to a lot of mud, water, or sand, which is kind of odd, considering that's exactly what side-by-sides are usually exposed to. One of the advantages of UTVs, though, is that you can buy one that is new enough to be under warranty.

The service schedule for Kei trucks is generally not quite as frequent, and their simple engines are easy to work on. But we are talking about a 25-year-old vehicle here. Expect things to go wrong, like worn-out cooling systems, rusted parts of the frame, and vacuum lines that need replacing. Parts are surprisingly easy to find, though you may have to order some of them online. But most of us who work on our own cars have often done that, anyway.

It's hard to compare apples to apples when we talk about the pricing for these vehicles. Any road-legal Kei truck you purchase in the U.S. will be at least 25 years old. It's not likely that you're going to look for a side-by-side that is that old. They are also built for different uses on different terrains.

You can find 25- to nearly 40-year-old Suzuki Carry trucks on Autotrader for anywhere from $7,000 to over $12,000. That's wild, considering you could get a brand-new Carry in Japan for around $7,500 to $10,000. On top of that, you're likely to have to make repairs right off the bat, since the truck is so old. A brand-new Polaris Ranger 1000 UTV costs more, starting around $15,000. But that comes with a 12-month warranty. We found late-model used UTVs on Autotrader and ATV Trader that were priced about the same as much older Kei trucks.

So, which is the better deal? Who's to say? If you're just looking at age and wear and how it lines up with total cost, side-by-sides have a definite advantage. But that doesn't mean they represent the better deal for you personally. Paying a little more for a vehicle that is ideally suited for your uses is a better deal than paying less for a vehicle that doesn't quite fit your needs. Do your research, evaluate how and where you'll use the vehicle, and then make the purchase that's right for you.

#5666. Zoox Launches Robotaxis in Atlanta

The year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas, I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!

“Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares.

To start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

In case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the company informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami, our public service in Las Vegas, and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco.”

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:

“Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”

Circling back to Atlanta and why the company has made that one of the first cities for its robotaxi deployment, Zoox adds the following: “Atlanta is a dynamic, vibrant city. Known as the ‘Silicon Valley of the South,’ it boasts one of the largest ride-hailing markets in the United States. Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”

Lastly, as I also highlighted in my article last night about Zoox expanding in Las Vegas, one key thing Zoox is proud of and argues sets it apart from the competition is how vertically integrated its robotaxi business is and how useful the design of its vehicle is for its purpose. Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. Unlike the retrofitted solutions currently on the road, our robotaxi was built from the ground up for fully autonomous ride-hailing. It has no steering wheel or driver’s seat, instead featuring spacious, carriage-style seating for up to four passengers. This design layout allows us to offer Zoox passengers more than just a ride; we are providing a private space where riders can socialize, relax, and reclaim their time. […]

“Zoox owns, operates, and assembles its vehicles, and is the only company currently deploying a fully driverless, purpose-built robotaxi on public roads in the U.S.

“We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”

You can learn more on the Zoox website or the Zoox app.

#5665. Secure Solar Futures set to install 313-kW array on Virginia elementary school

Secure Solar Futures, a commercial solar contractor, will build a 313-kW solar power system at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, Virginia. Construction of the system is expected to start later this year at no cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year power purchase agreement with Secure Solar Futures.

A total of 531 bifacial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, Texas, will be installed on the rooftop of the school, and the array is expected to offset 67% of the power used by the school annually. In its first year, the school’s solar system is projected to produce 421 MWh of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes.

Under the PPA, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy and Secure Solar Futures will own, operate and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

Preston Park Elementary School is expected to save $581,000 electricity costs over the term of the PPA. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s lifespan.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5664. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5663. 5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. The Impala SS (Super Sport) is a pure horsepower play that dates back to 1961, two years after the Bowtie brand launched the Impala as a standalone model. Its numbers are still impressive, even by 21st-century standards. The retail version of the Impala SS from the 1960s, which covered two generations, produced up to 425 horsepower. The later Impala SS generations from the 1990s and 2000s were less brutish, offering between 240 and 303 hp, but they were still a step up from their more mundane counterparts.

However, these horsepower numbers come with a catch. The output figures for 1960s Impala SS models reflected gross horsepower ratings, which generally didn't account for intake, exhaust, and accessory loads. When the 1970s rolled around, the auto industry was dealing with tighter emissions regulations and insurance companies that took a dim view of high-powered cars. By the 1972 model year, Detroit switched to net horsepower calculations to better reflect real-world engine configurations. Because gross horsepower ratings often varied from manufacturer to manufacturer, there's no standard way to convert horsepower ratings between the methods, but both still measure horsepower at the crankshaft, not the wheels.

Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net. Special race versions and modified cars are excluded. Here's how every Impala SS generation compares in maximum power output.

The first Impala was a variant of the 1958 Bel Air, but the SS designation didn't arrive until the third-generation Impala in 1961. The second generation, without a Super Sport option, filled the two-year gap as the free-standing Impala model. The first Impala SS model's power output is a story of progression. The 1961 Impala SS arrived with a choice of V8 engines: 348-cubic-inch units rated at 305, 340, or 350 horsepower and a 409-cubic-inch V8 officially rated at 360 horsepower. In 1962, that king-of-the-hill powerplant could also be configured with dual four-barrel carburetors, increasing output to 409 horsepower.

Thanks to solid lifters, dual exhausts, and an 11:1 compression ratio, the 409's output rose to 425 gross horsepower for the 1963 model year. Chevy history buffs may also recall a 1963 Z11 lightweight drag-racing Impala with a 430-horsepower 427-cubic-inch V8. Keep in mind that this one wasn't a Super Sport model, nor was it a part of regular production, as only 57 were ever produced. The 1964 Impala SS continued with the same 409 from the previous year.

Horsepower for the second iteration of the Impala SS was in familiar territory, with peak outputs sitting at 425, but the Impala eventually took a different route to get there. To start, Chevy launched an entirely new Impala with a sleeker exterior and a perimeter frame, ditching the X-type architecture of the outgoing model. The new looks helped the 1965 Impala become the best-selling single model of all time. A record 1,046,514 units were sold, with roughly 23% being SS variants. Impala SS examples from this generation still attract a lot of attention online.

The top engine for the non-SS 1965 Impala was the familiar Turbo-Fire 409-cubic-inch V8, making 400 horsepower. For the SS, Chevy also offered the L78 V8, a 396-cubic-inch V8 rated at 425 gross horsepower. A year later, the L72 427-cubic-inch V8 joined the options list, also rated for up to 425 hp. The powerplant featured a forged crankshaft and pistons, solid lifters, and a dual exhaust system. The SS 427 continued into 1967 and 1968, but with a slightly different L36 engine, still with 427 cubic inches, but now rated at 385 hp. In 1969, output increased to 390 hp.

The final Impala SS came with 303 hp, which is the most of any modern generation. The supercharged V6 in the previous eighth-generation SS was replaced with a naturally aspirated 5.3-liter LS4 V8. That results in a zero-to-60 mph dash of 5.6 seconds, which is on par with a modern-day Mazda Miata – but remember, this was 20 years ago.

That seems straightforward enough, but the final-generation Impala SS has some quirks that don't match its muscle-era badge. Notably, the ninth-generation Impala was front-wheel-drive, and naturally, so was the SS variant. Power traveled through a four-speed automatic transmission, albeit a heavy-duty version. Despite having an upgraded suspension that helped this SS go beyond a rental car-spec version, reviews of the day weren't particularly kind to the SS. In a 2006 road test, Car and Driver stated, "The SS seems to have been created to produce impressive numbers on paper with little regard to driver enjoyment." Nonetheless, the Impala SS's swan song continued through the 2009 model year.

After a quarter-century hiatus, Chevrolet resurrected the Impala SS for the 1994 model year. This time, it was packaged in a rear-wheel-drive sedan with a 260-horsepower 5.7-liter V8 engine under the hood. Engineers didn't have to dig too far into the parts bin. This LT1 V8 already saw duty in the Camaro and Corvette, although there are different LT1 versions over the years. However, the engine in the Impala SS was modified with cast-iron cylinder heads and a different camshaft. It was also tuned for more torque: 330 pound-feet in this application. By today's standards, a 0-to-60 mph dash of seven seconds is nothing exciting, but this was three decades ago, and this Impala SS weighed about 4,300 pounds.

That bulk came from the full-sized Caprice, which underpinned this seventh-generation version. In effect, you could say that Chevrolet made a civilian version of the Caprice police car. The vehicle included an upgraded suspension, improved cooling, larger disc brakes, and a limited-slip differential. The five-spoke aluminum wheels and subtle strips of exterior chrome trim helped distinguish this Impala from its workhorse siblings. Leather upholstery was another clue. For its final production year, 1996, the column-mounted shifter was moved to the center console, and a tachometer was added. That's why low-mileage 1996 Impala SS examples still hold strong collector appeal.

The short-lived eighth-generation Impala SS (2004–2005) stands out for a couple of reasons besides having the lowest engine output (240 horsepower). Namely, it's the only Impala SS with a V6 engine. Yet this is no ordinary six-cylinder powerplant; it's General Motors' 3.8-liter Series II engine with an Eaton supercharger, known for its broad torque band.

This Impala SS is based on the eighth-generation Impala, which was introduced for the 2000 model year as a front-wheel-drive sedan. Fast forward to 2004, and Chevrolet added the SS variant to the lineup, marking the first Impala SS that spins the front wheels. An upgraded four-speed automatic transmission controls the setup, but this Chevy also has larger anti-roll bars, modified springs, and Goodyear performance tires. As a result, 0-60 mph came in 6.5 seconds.

To go beyond a plain-Jane Impala, the automaker also added four round taillights (marketing language called this a Corvette-inspired treatment), black-only exterior paint, a small rear spoiler, leather upholstery, and a slathering of SS badges inside and out. This Impala was axed after 2005 to make way for the aforementioned 2006 Impala SS with a more powerful V8 engine.

#5662. Study Pinpoints States with Steepest Warming Trends Since 1980

The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

By Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, MIT

#5661. 12 Plug-In Hybrids With The Longest Electric-Only Range

Back in 2010, Chevrolet introduced the groundbreaking Volt — America's first plug-in hybrid production car. Packing a fairly big 16-kWh battery pack, the Volt had an EPA-estimated electric range of 35 miles, with later first-generation models rated at up to 38 miles. When the battery was depleted, it turned to a 1.4-liter four-cylinder engine with 84 horsepower to cover longer distances.

Although it ultimately failed to attract enough buyers and was discontinued in 2019, the Chevrolet Volt was so far ahead of its time that many current PHEVs struggle to match its electric range. In fact, out of the 12 plug-in hybrids with the longest electric-only range on sale right now, four have lower range figures. Of course, many modern PHEVs offer more EV range, with some models, like the 2027 Land Rover Range Rover Plug-in Hybrid, 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e 4MATIC, and 2027 Toyota RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid, capable of delivering 50 miles of driving without calling on the internal combustion engine.

To compile this list, we evaluated the 2027 plug-in hybrids for the U.S. market, ranking them from the shortest to longest electric range based on EPA estimates. For models awaiting official 2027 figures, we used their 2026 EPA ratings, noting any powertrain changes. Excluded are models that are all-new for 2027 and not yet EPA-rated. Also, all listed prices include the destination charge. Let's dig in!

The 2027 Kia Sportage is offered with three powertrains — a 2.5-liter gas engine with 187 hp, 1.6-liter turbo-four hybrid with 232 hp, and a plug-in variant with an electric motor for 268 hp combined. However, the PHEV's added potency doesn't translate into real-world performance, as it needs the same 6.9 seconds to reach 60 mph as the regular hybrid (per Car and Driver's testing procedure).

But this should surprise nobody, as the Sportage Plug-in Hybrid has a significantly larger and heavier 13.8-kWh battery, with the regular hybrid packing a small 1.5-kWh pack. As a result, it provides a meaningful EV-only range of 34 miles. The battery also supports Level 2 charging, so it can be fully recharged in only two hours. Once the battery is depleted, the Sportage Plug-in Hybrid doesn't turn into a gas guzzler and returns a respectable 36 mpg combined. Not bad, considering it also comes standard with AWD, unlike the gas and hybrid models, where AWD is optional.

Saving money on fuel by making the most of the PHEV's battery does require a few compromises, though. The Sportage Plug-in Hybrid starts at $42,085 in the X-Line trim, compared to $37,285 for the regular hybrid in the same trim. The hybrid Sportage is also available in lower-end trims, with the base LX costing $32,085.

The PHEV's larger battery also eats into cargo space. While the Sportage Hybrid has a big 39.5-cubic-foot trunk — only 0.1 cubic feet smaller than the gas model — the PHEV offers only 34.5 cubic feet of cargo capacity. Fortunately, there is no difference in passenger accommodation, with all Sportage models offering ample space for adults in both rows.

BMW facelifted the 7 Series for 2027, replacing the outgoing model's convoluted fascia with a cleaner front end that actually complements its monolithic, slab-sided proportions. As is customary nowadays, the cabin got a tech upgrade, with the 7 Series now packing BMW's Panoramic iDrive system with a parallelogram-like center screen, a thin panoramic display at the base of the windshield, and even a passenger screen. Meanwhile, passengers in the rear can now use the massive 31.3-inch theater-screen for Zoom video calls thanks to the built-in camera.

BMW also massaged the 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 in the 740, which now produces 394 hp (previously 375 hp). The 750e xDrive PHEV variant remains largely unchanged, though, packing the same 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 hybrid with 483 hp and 516 lb-ft of torque sent to all four wheels. It's a potent powertrain, bringing the luxury sedan to 60 mph in 4.6 seconds and up to an electronically limited top speed of 155 mph, which drops to 87 mph on EV power alone.

Arriving next year, the 2027 750e xDrive hasn't yet received its official EPA figures. However, it should be rated close to the 2026 model's 35 miles, as they share the same powertrain. The 2026 750e xDrive is also rated at 24 mpg once the battery is depleted, for a total range of 460 miles. BMW hasn't announced pricing for the 2027 model yet, but expect a slight bump over the 2026 version's $111,550 starting price.

The 2028 Volvo XC60 will offer more electric range than any other PHEV when it arrives in spring next year. Packing a large battery pack with a 37.9-kWh usable capacity, the heavily refreshed XC60 will cover 78 miles on electricity alone, more than enough for covering all daily driving errands, apart from the occasional long trip. In that case, the driver can always utilize the 2.0-liter turbo-four engine and expand the range to 590 miles.

With such astonishing numbers, the refreshed XC60 makes you think twice about buying the current model. With a smaller 14.7-kWh (usable) pack, the 2027 Volvo XC60 Plug-in Hybrid has enough juice for an EPA-estimated range of 35 miles. That's still in line with current offerings in the PHEV space, but, damn, the 2028 model makes a massive case for itself with that EV-like range. Let's hope it doesn't cost much more than the 2027 XC60 PHEV's $67,595 starting price, because batteries are expensive.

The refreshed XC60 Plug-in Hybrid will also be more potent, producing 455 horsepower. The current model is no slouch, though. With 401 hp on tap, courtesy of an electrically assisted 2.0-liter turbo-four, the XC60 PHEV needs only 4.6 seconds to reach 60 mph. The PHEV powertrain is hooked to an eight-speed automatic and standard AWD. The XC60 offers decent interior room, though the PHEV's 21.1-cubic-foot cargo capacity is on the small side for the category. The cabin design is classically minimalist.

Lexus gave the NX a comprehensive mid-cycle overhaul for 2027, ditching the 2.4-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine in favor of an all-hybrid lineup. Crucially, the plug-in hybrid NX 450h+ comes with a next-gen powertrain with more power and an 8% larger battery. Lexus estimates a 45-mile range for the new model, a significant jump from the 37-mile EPA-estimated range of the 2026 model.

Even if the EPA range turns out to be lower than Lexus' estimate, the 2027 NX 450h+ is worth the wait, with the first models arriving by the end of this year. For instance, while the ample interior space hasn't changed, there is a new, classier dashboard that comes standard with a 14.0-inch touchscreen and a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster. Lexus says it also improved the driving dynamics, though in our first drive, we found that the Lexus NX doubles down on quiet luxury rather than chasing sportiness.

That said, the 2027 NX 450h+ should be a bit quicker, packing 324 horsepower thanks to a more powerful front motor-generator. With 304 hp on tap, the 2026 NX 450h+ sprints to 60 mph in 6.0 seconds, with the 2027 model expected to drop a few tenths. Pricing for the 2027 NX is unknown at the moment, but it will almost certainly creep past the $59,505 starting figure of the 2026 model.

In 2005, Lexus followed its parent company Toyota's lead by introducing the RX 400h — the world's first luxury hybrid vehicle. Since then, every generation of Lexus' luxury crossover has been available as a hybrid, with the current RX available with three distinct electrified powertrains: RX 350h, RX 450h+, and RX 500h.

The RX 450h+ is the first plug-in hybrid RX, combining a 2.5-liter gas engine with three electric motors for an output of 304 hp. As a result, the 2027 RX 450h+ sprints to 60 mph in 6.2 seconds. It also comes standard with AWD, enabled via an electric motor on the rear axle. With an 18.1-kWh battery onboard, the RX 450h+ has a solid EPA-estimated range of 38 miles. Thanks to Toyota's efficient series-parallel hybrid system, the plug-in RX sips fuel with a 35-mpg combined EPA rating once the battery is depleted.

The interior of the latest RX is luxurious and tech-forward, with an available 14.0-inch infotainment screen housing physical knobs and on-screen buttons for HVAC control. The cabin is more than spacious enough for adults in both seating rows, with a good 30-cubic-foot cargo volume — the same as on the RX 350h hybrid with the smaller battery. The RX 450h+ starts at $66,880 for the Premium trim, driving the price up considerably over the regular hybrid's $57,750 with the same equipment.

The fabled Mercedes-AMG E63 nameplate was discontinued in 2022, taking with it the 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8. But Mercedes-AMG didn't want to give up on the idea of a high-performance E-Class, so it used a novel plug-in hybrid powertrain in the latest E 53 Hybrid.

Combining a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 with 443 horsepower and a 161-hp synchronous electric motor, AMG's PHEV produces 577 hp as standard, or up to 604 hp with the Dynamic Plus Package and RACE START mode — 1 hp more than its V8 predecessor. The E 53 AMG Hybrid comes standard with AWD and a 9-speed automatic, reaching 60 mph in just 3.9 seconds.

Yes, this new high-performance E-Class won't sing V8 harmonics to your ears, but it has another trick up its sleeve: a big 28.6-kWh (21.2 kWh usable) ultra-lightweight high-performance battery. As a result, the E 53 AMG has an EPA-estimated EV range of up to 44 miles (2026 model), or 41 miles for the wagon.

Did we say a wagon? Yup, the E 53 AMG is also available in wagon form in the U.S., which should probably be the model you go for, as it has significantly more cargo space. Both models offer excellent cabin space, but due to the large battery, the sedan has a comically small 12.7-cubic-foot trunk. The wagon rectifies that with a much more usable 33.1-cubic-foot trunk, while delivering a 3.8-second 0 to 60 mph sprint with RACE START. The sedan E 53 AMG Hybrid starts at $92,550, while the wagon will set you back $96,650.

The hybrid pioneer has been significantly revamped for the current generation, transforming from the industry's ugly duckling to possibly the best-looking car on the market, with a sleek, coupe-like silhouette and athletic proportions.

Naturally, the Prius is a hybrid-only affair, available with a regular or plug-in hybrid powertrain. The former is an efficiency king, rated at up to 55 mpg combined by the EPA, while the latter provides an EPA-estimated electric range of up to 44 miles from a relatively small 13.6-kWh battery.

Because it's over 350 pounds heavier, the Prius PHEV is rated at a lower 51 mpg combined once the battery is depleted, which is still an impressive figure. The Prius PHEV is more powerful, though, producing 220 hp from its 2.0-liter hybrid powertrain. As a result, it accelerates to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds, a solid figure for a family car. Unfortunately, while the regular hybrid is available with FWD and AWD, the Prius PHEV is FWD-only.

Due to the Prius PHEV's coupe-like shape, the rear bench is short on headroom, and knee room isn't particularly stellar, either. Still, the 20.3-cubic-foot trunk is decently sized for a compact family car. Also, while the 12.3-inch (8.0-inch standard) touchscreen houses most of the functions, the climate control buttons are physical.

Mercedes-Benz has thoroughly refreshed the S-Class for the 2027 model year, giving it a new design, advanced micro-LED headlights that provide better illumination without blinding other drivers, and of course, a new MBUX Superscreen infotainment with three separate screens and three built-in AI agents: Microsoft Bing Search, Google Cloud Automotive AI Agent, and ChatGPT-4o. Also, like in the latest 7 Series, rear passengers in the 2027 S-Class can now take video calls.

What a time to be alive, right? Hey, at least Mercedes-Benz improved other parts of the S-Class, like the plug-in hybrid powertrain in the S 580e 4MATIC variant. The outgoing 2026 model combines a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 with a 161-horsepower electric motor and pumps out 502 hp. Thanks to its 22-kWh battery, it has an EPA-estimated range of 47 miles. The 2027 model keeps the same battery capacity, but bumps the output to 576 hp. So, while the range stays the same, the new model will be quicker off the line. That extra performance pushes the price up to $136,150, compared to $131,750 for the outgoing car.

Unfortunately, the 2027 S 580e 4MATIC doesn't solve the biggest gripe of the 2026 model: the tight 8.1-cubic-foot cargo capacity. Mercedes-Benz lists the new car's trunk at 9 cubic feet, which is simply too small for a high-end luxury sedan.

Want a PHEV with a long EV range and more cargo capacity? The Range Rover P550e Plug-in Hybrid can swallow much more cargo than the S 580e in its 40.7-cubic-foot trunk, while also offering an EPA-estimated range of 50 miles thanks to its sizeable 38.2-kWh (31.8-kWh usable) battery pack. With a base price of $131,350, it's also cheaper than the 2027 S-Class PHEV.

Naturally, the Range Rover PHEV provides ample space for adults in both rows, though you can't have it in long-wheelbase, three-row form. Not that you'll miss much, as the rearmost seats in three-row Range Rovers are only fit for kids. As you'd expect from a Range Rover, the cabin is laden with high-quality materials. But it won't flood you with massive screens, packing a 13.1-inch infotainment screen and a 12-inch digital instrument cluster on its clean, minimalist dashboard.

The Range Rover P550e offers more than enough performance for a luxury SUV. The powertrain centers on a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 and an eight-speed automatic, producing 543 horsepower after the electric boost. Land Rover says this is enough to move the 6,025-pound behemoth to 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and up to a top speed of 150 mph. The powertrain's efficiency isn't its forte, though, as it's only rated at 21 mpg combined once the battery is depleted.

The smaller, sporty variant of the Range Rover Plug-in Hybrid comes in two flavors: P460e and P550e. Both are based on a 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-6 engine and one electric motor, but differ in power output. The P460e is good for 454 horsepower and a 0 to 60 mph sprint of 5.3 seconds. Meanwhile, the P550e matches its larger sibling with 543 hp and drops the acceleration figure down to 4.7 seconds.

Both PHEVs share their larger sibling's battery pack, with 31.8 kWh of usable capacity, good for an EPA-estimated range of 53 miles. Still, they are significantly cheaper, with the P460e starting at $96,950, while the P550e is only available with the Battersea Edition trim, which includes goodies like a rear limited-slip differential and 22-inch forged wheels, and costs $113,850.

The Range Rover Sport has a similar interior design as the Range Rover, with an identical two-display approach and high-quality materials. Both rows offer ample space for passengers, though unlike the larger model, the Sport isn't available in three-row form with any powertrain. Since it's smaller, the Range Rover Sport has less cargo capacity: 31.9 cubic feet.

With a starting price of $64,150, the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e 4MATIC is more expensive than the 2026 Lexus NX 450h+ ($59,505), but it also houses a larger 24.8-kWh (23.3-kWh usable) battery pack that provides an EPA-estimated range of 54 miles. The GLC 350e also supports 60-kW DC fast charging, enough to take the battery from 10 to 80% in just 20 minutes. Still, Merc's hybrid powertrain can't compete with the efficiency of Toyota's hybrids, with the GLC 350e 4MATIC delivering 25 mpg once the battery is depleted.

Based on a 2.0-liter turbo-four, Merc's plug-in powertrain is more potent, too, producing 313 hp. Mercedes-Benz says that's enough for a 0 to 60 mph time of 6.3 seconds, slightly slower than the NX's 6.0 seconds. The GLC 350e 4MATIC comes standard with AWD and a 9-speed automatic, which some buyers might prefer over the NX's e-CVT.

Inside, the Mercedes-Benz GLC pampers passengers with ample space in both rows and premium materials throughout. Its 22-cubic-foot trunk is also reasonably sized for a compact SUV with a fairly large battery. Unlike most modern Mercedes-Benz vehicles, the GLC 350e comes with a relatively small 11.9-inch infotainment screen in the middle, paired with a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster.

The 2026 Toyota RAV4 arrived as an all-hybrid model ready to once again dominate its category. With a new design and a powertrain lineup consisting of Toyota's fifth-gen hybrid and sixth-gen PHEV powertrains, the latest RAV4 bets on efficiency. A year later, Toyota further improved the RAV4 formula by equipping every PHEV trim with a NACS port and support for DC fast charging.

The powertrain itself remained largely unchanged, though. Based around a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine and three electric motors (AWD), it produced 324 hp in 2026 form, enough for a 0 to 60 mph time of just 5.4 seconds. That's quick for a compact crossover, with Toyota even launching the fun-to-drive RAV4 GR Sport variant around this powertrain. As per Toyota's estimates, the entry-level 2027 RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid SE has a range of 52 miles. Still, the 2026 model is rated at an EPA-estimated 54 miles, although Toyota initially estimated a shorter 52-mile range.

The latest RAV4 can comfortably accommodate adults in both rows, while boasting a 33.5-cubic-foot trunk. Its dashboard is now more tech-forward, with a standard 10.5-inch touchscreen powered by Toyota's latest Arene software platform. The 2027 RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid starts at $43,695 for the SE trim, an increase of $600 over the 2026 model.

#5660. AI Businesses Still Bleeding Billions

AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions quickly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally).

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

One might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the company’s revenue was actually up by 50%! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

OpenAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

Frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?

As we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?

The one big player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

“The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings. In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble.”

Why can’t the leaders of these companies just ask their chatbots how to turn a profit and implement their answers? Well, one of the answers might have been regulatory capture and blocking others from entering the market, but that dream may now be out the window. In my humble opinion, 2027 could be a very interesting year for AI companies, and that might involve a big popping noise.

Zach is tryin' to help society help itself one word at a time. He spends most of his time here on CleanTechnica as its editor-in-chief and CEO. Zach is recognized globally as an electric vehicle, solar energy, and energy storage expert. He has presented about electric vehicles and renewable energy at conferences in India, the UAE, Ukraine, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, the USA, Canada, and Curaçao.

#5659. Toyota Could Finally Bring The Perfect S-FR Concept To Production With The Help Of Daihatsu

Back in 2015, Toyota teased us with the perfect car: The S-FR concept, a Miata-fighting two-door roadster set to be a little sibling to what was then the Scion FR-S. After that big reveal, the little car just vanished into thin air, never to be seen again except in my most beautiful and hopeful dreams. Now, though, it seems those winds could be changing once again. A new report out of Japan says that Toyota is thinking about finally bringing the S-FR to production.

The news comes from Japanese outlet Response, which said the S-FR could finally hit dealerships as early as 2027, though not quite as it was originally designed. Instead of being a Miata fighter, the new S-FR would be even smaller, built on the platform of a third-generation Daihatsu Copen. Daihatsu teased a new Copen with its K-Open concept last year (pictured below), and it wouldn't be hard for Toyota to throw a bit of design work at its subsidiary's kei car and bring a proper S-FR to market.

Of course, a modern kei car would be a pretty substantial rework of the S-FR formula. Previous Copens have all been front-wheel drive, so shifting to a rear-wheel-drive platform to accommodate an S-FR twin would make it more of a sports car, too. The original concept was neither modern nor kei, with a 1.5-liter naturally-aspirated four-cylinder engine and a rear seat, the former of which would be impossible and the latter unlikely in a kei car. In fact, the whole design would need to shrink to meet kei car requirements, making it even less likely we'd get a version here in the States. Still, Toyota is already bringing us one kei, so maybe we can dream.

Even if it's only for the Japanese market, I hope this report from Response is accurate and that Toyota is really thinking about bringing the S-FR to market as a Copen variant. It just makes sense — take your beloved-but-abandoned little sports car concept and apply it to your soon-to-be-resurrected little sports car platform. Maybe, if we're really lucky, Toyota will bring some over to the States as the same sort of low-speed vehicle as the KEI-01. I'd happily tune a limiter out of one of these just to get to drive it.
