#5658. Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach

MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering, the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team’s computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.”

Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of human-caused carbon emissions.

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

Concrete is strong when compressed, but weak when pulled, so it’s reinforced with steel that can handle the pulling forces. The researchers first mapped a path for the steel reinforcement using a method called graphic statics, which can generate structural designs almost instantly. They used it to shape the steel bar so that it carries an equal share of the weight along its entire length to keep the reinforcement simple enough for builders to make. Topology optimization, which works more slowly but can place material freely, was used to determine where concrete was needed and where material could be removed from areas where it contributes little to the structural performance.

“Both methods are good at different things, so we tried to combine the strengths of both into a single methodology,” says Jewett.

The resulting beam has a top section, narrow angled legs, and a thin bottom section for the steel reinforcement. The team’s automated process translated the 3D beam design into flat fabric pieces that can be cut and sewn into a mold, accounting for how the fabric will deform once concrete is poured in. A simple timber frame supported the finished fabric mold.

For Mark Hellrich SM ’26, the study’s lead author, the main hands-on challenge was getting the concrete mix right. Woven cotton fabric lets water seep through, so a mix that is too runny loses water through the mold. It also presses harder against the fabric, pushing it away from the intended shape.

The team used a moderately wet, sand-rich mix with only small stones, so the concrete could flow through the beam’s narrow, angled legs and thin bottom section without getting stuck. They then packed it in by hand, prodding each layer and tapping and kneading the fabric from the outside.

“This is where the flexibility of the mold becomes an advantage: you can work the concrete through the interconnected passages without a vibrator, which a rigid mold of this shape would need,” says Hellrich. A concrete vibrator is a tool typically used to shake air pockets out of freshly poured concrete in rigid molds.

Once the concrete was in place, the wet fabric revealed the beam’s final shape. “All three beams were free of wrinkles and creases,” says Hellrich. The top surface stayed close to the design, while the main difference was a downward sag along the bottom, with the angled legs folding slightly inward.

To find out how much sewing precision the beam needs, the team built three molds for the same design, made from 36, 56, and 76 fabric pieces. Comparing the 3D scans of the cast beams with the target design, the researchers found that more seams gave finer control over the details, but did not necessarily make the beam’s overall shape more accurate.

“More seams improve local control because they divide the fabric into smaller, more constrained panels. But a more complex pattern also has more pieces to align and more seam length, so small cutting, sewing, and assembly inaccuracies can accumulate across the mold, explains Carstensen.

The 56-piece mold demonstrated the best balance, capturing the important design geometry without the added time, effort, and potential errors associated with the most complex pattern.

The researchers then load-tested one of the beams, gradually stacking 36 water-filled buckets on top of it, up to about 30 percent of its design load to reflect everyday service conditions. Weighted lines hung from the beam’s underside to precise measuring gauges below, tracking how far the beam bent as the load was added and removed. At the beam’s center, the measured deflection — its downward movement under the load — was within about 2 percent of the computer model’s prediction.

The team also compared the cost of a single fabric-formed beam with a conventional one and found that location makes all the difference. In the Global South, where materials tend to cost more relative to labor, all three fabric versions were cheaper, with savings of about 10 to 20 percent. In the Global North, higher labor costs for sewing reversed that advantage, making the fabric versions about 16 to 55 percent more expensive.

The findings suggest that fabric formwork is most promising for custom-shaped concrete components produced as a one-off or in small batches, such as exposed beams, roof or long-span framing, pedestrian structures, and landscape elements. For the repetitive, rectangular beams found in most buildings, conventional reusable molds remain the more economical choice where labor is expensive.

“To get started, a builder would need the digital pattern for the target component, a sewing machine and suitable fabric, and a simple timber support frame,” Carstensen says. “That is a much lower equipment threshold than robotic fabrication, concrete 3D printing, or CNC-milled molds.”

The researchers describe the 3-meter beam as a proof of concept comparable to a short building span. It is also a big step up from the 1.2-meter beam the team built in a previous project, Jewett notes.

Building bigger isn’t just a matter of enlarging the design, Carstensen notes. As a beam gets longer, its own weight and the pressure on the fabric mold change, so a larger beam would need a new design. The next step, Carstensen says, is “to test multiple beams to failure.”

“The nice thing about these optimization methods is they generate structures that look organic,” Jewett says. “Their geometries are clear expressions of how the forces move through the structural system. There is elegance to them. It makes you ask why we don’t design all our structures in this way.”

Joining Carstensen, Jewett, and Hellrich on the paper are co-authors Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, and Emily Whiting, of Boston University’s Department of Computer Science.

The work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

By Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, MIT

#5657. SOLRITE and sonnen collaborate on integrated VPP breaker

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5656. $3.4 Billion — Anthropic Order for Gas Power Plants!

Wow, this is a nasty, dirty, polluting stunner I didn’t see until just now.

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has reportedly signed a $3.4 billion contract to buy gas-fired engines (power plants) from OnePWR Solutions, a Texas-based energy company. These gas power plants would be able to provide Anthropic’s AI data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity — with the real cost being an enormous amount of air pollution and global warming emissions.

If you thought Anthropic was supposed to be “the good guy” in the AI industry, perhaps think again.

The Financial Times, which broke the news on this, says that this is the “largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.” It’s this line from Futurism that really sums up my feelings: “It isn’t just symptomatic of a desperate race to secure the necessary utilities: it’s also one of the clearest signs yet that the AI industry has turned its back on the growing climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing gas generators it’s installing across the globe.” Indeed. It’s one thing to be racing to be a leader in this field, but to turn to polluting, climate-destroying gas power plants instead of solar and wind power, that’s absolutely disappointing and — frankly — morally disgusting.

For the heck of it, to see what this company’s AI bot thought about the power choice it made, I decided to ask Claude “Are gas power plants harmful to our climate?” The response was as follows:

“Yes, though they’re less harmful than coal and more harmful than most alternatives.

“Bottom line: Gas is a cleaner fossil fuel, not a clean one. Its climate impact is best judged by what it replaces (coal vs. renewables) and by how tightly methane leaks are controlled. Carbon capture could reduce plant emissions, but it’s still costly and not widely deployed.”

So, yeah, when you’re choosing to buy $3.4 billion worth of gas power plants instead of renewable energy power plants, that is without a doubt going to be a horrible decision for our climate. I’m sure if I asked Claude about the risk humans race from climate change, the answer would not be uplifting. But I’m not going to go there. Instead, I’ll turn back to Futurism for this summary: “Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating. And the prognosis for the future is grim. Last month, environmental nonprofit Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, wiping out nearly 15 years worth of greenhouse gas reduction efforts.”

Indeed — we’re facing drastic increases in emissions from the very dirty AI industry. The good news is people are already showing they’re fed up with AI data centers. Apparently, out of 41 ballot measures related to data centers that were up for a vote in the recent midterm elections, only one (1) went the way of the AI industry. That said, I don’t see investments in growth stopping right now, as is evidenced by this $3.4 billion gas engine order and OpenAI and others burning through billions of dollars a quarter.

#5655. What's Your Most Unforgettable Close Call?

People are capable of doing some supremely stupid things in cars. We've seen the warnings from informational videos over the decades, and our personal blunders and experiences have demonstrated this point, too. We can, of course, be attentive behind the wheel, but that doesn't account for the others who aren't while on the road. It's partly why dash cams and their resulting videos have gained so much traction in recent years. While someone's dumb decision may end up in disaster, others might end in close calls — moments where destruction was inches away.

Close calls happen more often than you might expect, especially when we live in an era where vehicles are equipped with every warning along with literal bells and whistles to tell drivers they might hit something. This week, we don't want to know about the little near-misses — we want to know about the big ones that haunt you. Tell us about the misses that had they been hits, would've made for calamity.

Years ago, while in the city for the New York International Auto Show, I was lucky enough to be driving a well-equipped 2021 Maserati Levante GTS. I had taken it on a scenic drive along the Belt Parkway to Amityville, and on my return to Brooklyn, I hit a bit of traffic. About 10 minutes into my drive, in a 35 mph residential zone, an Audi Q5 came speeding up behind me. I reactively slowed down to let it fly past.

I watched as this Q5 blazed through a red light and hit another car, a fairly new Subaru, before the Q5 went spinning into the other side of the intersection. That was near miss number one. Two people got out of the smashed Q5 and bolted. Instinctively, I wanted to stop and help, but I was in a part of New York I was unfamiliar with in a six-figure vehicle that wasn't mine. Instead, I opted to get around the scene.

Seconds later, a Ford Taurus came up on my bumper, then quickly maneuvered ahead to cut me off before making a turn into a parking lot where it then stopped, and a cop hopped out and proceeded to stop a kid who had run from the crash scene. The Taurus was never put in park, though, and it started rolling towards the Maserati. I panicked, trying to figure out how to reverse it with its weird shifter.

The cop saw what was happening and was able to catch the car about an inch away from the Maserati. Near miss number two. Meanwhile, another cop had arrested the kid. After a deep breath and a phone call to my husband, still quite shaken, I made my way back to Brooklyn.

It might not have been the greatest near-miss, but the feelings I had nearly five years ago remain strong to this day. With that chaos in mind, what was your most unforgettable close call? Tell us all about it and why it holds critical space in your memory bank in the comments below.

#5654. What The US Midterm Elections Mean For Climate Progress

People across the United States voted in record numbers in last week’s incredibly consequential election, which has completely changed the makeup of Congress for its new term beginning in January 2027. The success of our electoral processes—still underway—should not be taken for granted. It’s a win for democracy when millions of citizens peacefully claim their right to a government of, by, and for the people.

Will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this new Congress? That remains to be seen, and I’m not holding my breath. But there’s no question that the shift in Congress has significant implications for the administration’s ability to continue to ram through its anti-science, authoritarian agenda—including on climate and clean energy issues.

Energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers, and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted. While not everyone explicitly named climate change as a top issue (although many did put it in their top three), its fingerprints are all over the issues a majority of voters did name in polls.

If you care about addressing the high costs of electricity and gas, then you must reckon with the fact that this current fossil energy crisis, unleashed by the Trump administration’s war against Iran, is an extreme manifestation of the risks of fossil fuel dependence. The benefits of a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy—renewable energy that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked, further driving up costs for consumers—are tremendous. If you are deeply concerned about the rapid, unregulated build-out of data centers, you know that it comes with huge risks for communities related to climate, water, pollution, health, and electricity cost burdens. And it’s so clear that the Trump administration’s corruption, lies about climate science, and massive giveaways to fossil fuel polluters are leaving us all bearing the high costs of climate damages while large corporations and the president’s inner circle are raking in enormous profits.

Here’s another reality: regardless of politics, climate change is here, and science shows it’s rapidly worsening with the world’s imminent overshoot of 1.5°C of global warming. Communities are already experiencing deadly and costly climate impacts, including extreme heatwaves, catastrophic wildfires, record-breaking flooding, drought, accelerating sea level rise, intense ocean heat, irreversible loss of glaciers and ice sheets, stresses to critical ecosystems and more. These impacts are showing up in people’s daily lives—harming their health, destroying homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure, raising insurance premiums, hammering businesses, stressing water supplies, and threatening food security and affordability.

Climate change and clean energy are pocketbook issues. They are a lot more than that, of course. And climate change does not care if you live in a red state or a blue state. (One can ask if that is that even a relevant frame after an election that scrambled all conventional wisdom about “red” and “blue” dichotomies.)

Importantly, we will soon have a Congress where a majority accepts the scientific evidence on climate change. (Yes, I also wish we could take that for granted in 2026, but not in US politics, sadly.) That’s an important start and means we can advocate for policymakers to legislate based on the facts, instead of being stuck fighting disinformation and lies.

Here’s what this seismic “change election” could mean for action on climate change, some cautions about what likely won’t change right away, and what we’ll have to keep fighting for.

We will have to keep fighting back in courts to hold the Trump administration accountable for egregiously flouting the law. We’ve already had a major win in a lawsuit where the administration was found to be violating the Federal Advisory Committee Act in secretly setting up a ‘Climate Working Group’ stacked with climate contrarians to draft a sham science report, which the EPA then used to justify its proposal to gut the Endangerment Finding. We’ve also filed suit against the administration for repealing the Endangerment Finding, contrary to law, science, and the public interest.

On the international front, the Trump administration has shamefully exited the bedrock UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and that won’t change as long as it is in power. As I write from COP31 in Türkiye, the administration’s abandonment of global climate cooperation is very much on my mind; it’s crucial for the rest of the world to forge ahead regardless of the high stakes. There is a real risk that a beleaguered Trump administration will double down on its authoritarian ways and continue to find new ways to disrupt global climate progress and multilateral institutions. But Congress now has the power and responsibility to keep this reckless administration in check and ensure it is held accountable, at home and on the global stage.

“Change elections” come weighted with the hopes and dreams of many. As climate justice advocates, we know that policymakers have pushed off meaningful climate action far too long, and those failures are putting us all at profound risk. Yet, deep-pocketed fossil fuel interests, Big Tech, and other powerful entities continue to obstruct and delay action, still hold all too much sway over both parties in Congress, and we can expect their harmful tactics to ratchet up. So now it’s our responsibility to fight for what comes next, to make our shared dreams come true. Because those dreams of a safer, more just world for generations of young people to come must become reality.

#5653. Which Highway Really Has The Highest Number Of Lanes?

Freeways are to people what arteries are to red blood cells. Most freeways consist of three or four lanes of synchronized traffic flow (or collective halt), but have you ever wondered what the world record is for the highest number of lanes on a freeway? The obvious choice would be the Katy Freeway on I-10 just west of Houston, which has no fewer than 26 traffic lanes spread across both directions at its widest. However, that number also includes feeder roads that don't actually form part of the I-10, so it's often argued that the "true" number is actually 18.

If that's the case, a few other massive highways may indeed lay claim to Katy's title as the highest-lane highway in the world. Canada, for instance, has an 18-lane road approaching one of its airports, while Burma's capital city has a section with up to 20 lanes. However, perhaps the biggest threats sit halfway across the globe in China. These include a special section of the G4 Beijing–Hong Kong-Macau Expressway and the Hefei–Nanjing Expressway, the latter of which can open up to as many as 36 separate lanes — but with one very important caveat. Let's take a look at some of the highest-lane freeways in the world and how they compare before crowning the winner.

See, this is where things get tricky. While Katy has at least 18 lanes of moving traffic at its widest, both the G4's 25-lane and the Hefei–Nanjing Expressway's 36-lane sections are actually toll crossings. For example, the G4's 25-lane Zhuozhou Toll Gate section only starts about 710 yards before the tollbooths and ends about a quarter-mile after them. Most of its 1,412-mile road network — long, but not quite enough to match the world's longest highways — is actually just four lanes in each direction. The same goes for Hefei–Nanjing Expressway, which funnels back to four lanes beyond the 36-lane Wuzhuang Toll Gate.

That's the key differentiator here. By comparison, Katy's 18 lanes consist of 12 passenger car lanes and a maximum of six for high-occupancy vehicles (HOVs), and stretches for an estimated length of 12 miles. Of course, the definition for how long a stretch of road would need to be to qualify is subjective, but what isn't subjective is the fact that one has fast-moving traffic, and the others don't. In fact, back in 2015, huge delays at the G4's Zhuozhou crossing during China's Golden Week celebrations, with drivers stacked next to each other, gave rise to false reports that the G4 had as many as 50 lanes. Still, calling a slow-moving toll plaza a highway is a stretch. But what about other highways with 18+ lanes?

If you thought Germany's Autobahn, the only highway in the world with no speed limit, staked a claim, then you'd be quite wrong. Despite its infamous reputation, the Autobahn never goes above four lanes in each direction. The 20-lane section of Yaza Htarni Road in Naypyidaw, Burma, does count, though. It was brought to widespread attention during the "Top Gear: Burma Special" episode, where James, Jeremy, and Richard were astonished at just how wide (and empty) it was. However, it only extends for about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers); it's not an actual highway, and it's mostly deserted.

Then there's the King's Highway 401 in Ontario, which matches the Katy Freeway's 18 lanes as it approaches the Pearson International Airport. This sounds particularly useful given that the highway can sometimes see up to 500,000 vehicles over the course of a day. However, at the end of the day, none of these roads really match Katy at its widest, where feeder and carpool lanes join it to form as many as 26 lanes of fast-moving traffic.

#5652. 5 Four-Cylinder Engines With Terrible Reputations For Reliability

Four-cylinder engines come with their own set of pros and cons, just like six-, eight-, ten-, and even twelve-cylinder designs. Today, four-cylinder engines are the workhorses of the industry, powering everything from inexpensive daily drivers to luxury cars and high-performance models. Their appeal lies largely in a balance of efficiency, packaging, performance, and cost — but that same appeal means they're built in enormous numbers and pushed through a huge range of operating conditions.

In addition, engine development has grown increasingly complex in the modern age. Forced induction, hybrid systems, and sophisticated electronics have all added layers of engineering that simply didn't exist to the same degree a generation ago. But even without these factors, designing an engine capable of running flawlessly for decades is an extraordinarily difficult task.

Every engine contains components that eventually wear out, and the line between an expected maintenance item and a genuine engineering or manufacturing defect can sometimes be hard to draw. In other cases, though, the problem is impossible to ignore. Excessive oil consumption, failed head gaskets, damaged bearings, overheating, and catastrophic internal failures can turn an otherwise promising engine into one owners learn to avoid.

Because the engine is the heart of any vehicle, major failures can quickly damage the reputation of both the powertrain and the company that built it. And since four-cylinders are generally known for their reliability, the bad ones stand out even more. That's why some four-cylinder engines have become especially notorious for recurring defects, expensive repairs, and widespread owner complaints. Here are our picks of the five biggest offenders.

One Theta II engine problem from Hyundai and Kia is a prime example of the worst things that can go wrong. In 2015, Hyundai recalled (15V-568) around 470,000 units of the 2011/2012 Sonata equipped with either the 2.0-liter or the 2.4-liter Theta II inline-4 engine. Hyundai built the affected engines at its Alabama plant, where machining work on the engine's crankshaft left metal debris behind.

NHTSA's filing ties that debris to potential connecting rod bearing failure, and lists a knocking sound or an illuminated CEL as the warning signs before the engine dies. To say the least, customers didn't take that well since it led to an approval of a massive $1.3 billion settlement. For example, on CarComplaints, the 2016 Sonata's engine complaints carry a severity rating of "Really Awful," with an average failure mileage of just 24,456 miles and more than 1,000 complaints filed against the engine alone.

On the same site, the 2011 Sonata's seized engine ranks as the No. 1 Sonata engine problem, costing an average of $5,100 to fix at around 96,000 miles. J.D. Power's 2014 Vehicle Dependability Study, which surveyed owners of three-year-old 2011 models, also placed Hyundai among the bottom five brands, with a disappointing 169 problems per 100 vehicles, on average. Separately from the civil settlement, NHTSA announced consent orders against both Kia and Hyundai in 2020, penalizing them a combined $210 million.

These penalties followed an NHTSA review that concluded the recall covering the 1.6 million-plus Theta II vehicles had come too late, compounded by paperwork Hyundai and Kia filed with the agency that didn't hold up. This engine's reputation is so severe that enthusiasts on Reddit point to the Theta inline-4s as among the least reliable engines, and we even included it in our list of the worst engines of all time.

Do you know what's worse for an engine than metal shavings? Fire. This is exactly what plagued Ford's 1.6-liter EcoBoost. NHTSA's 2012 filing for a recall (12V-336) covered roughly 9,320 Escapes with an engine compartment fuel line that may have been damaged during assembly. However, that was not enough to fix the problem of engines bursting into flames. Two months later, a separate recall of 6,146 examples was issued (12V-431) over a different issue entirely: escaping antifreeze that could ignite. One would think that this would be it, but it was not. Three months later, another recall (12V-551) expanded the fire recall to more than 80,000 Escapes and Fusions over coolant leaks reaching the hot exhaust system.

By November 2013, Ford issued two more recalls on the same day. One (13V-583) covered 139,917 Escapes for yet another failure mode: overheating cracking the cylinder head and letting oil find its way out onto hot surfaces. The other (13V-584) covered the same vehicles from the original 12V-336 recall, because the replacement fuel line had, in some cases, been installed incorrectly the first time. Then, in 2017, another recall (17V-209) was issued for fire problems, covering 208,584 vehicles powered by the 1.6-liter.

It is not all about recalls though. The 1.6-liter is also prone to coolant intrusion, which Ford Authority called "very common with EcoBoost four-cylinder powerplants" after its tech found it in a 1.6-liter 2014 Escape. Plenty of owners on forums are dissatisfied, too, with one Bronco Sport Forum member echoing that "it's not a matter of IF but WHEN you will get coolant intrusion and have to do major engine work." Ford, it seems, is back at it with problems – five Ford models were just recalled for an EcoBoost engine problem, this time over faulty piston manufacturing in the 1.5-liter and 2.3-liter units.

The 2017 Nissan's VC-Turbo was the world's first production engine capable of adjusting its own compression ratio on the fly, but its positive reputation crumbled soon after. In June 2025, Nissan filed the first recall tied to the VC-Turbo family. 25V-437 covered 443,899 Rogues, Altimas, and Infiniti models, spanning both the 1.5-liter three-cylinder and 2.0-liter four-cylinder versions of the engine, over bearings that can fail outright.

That wasn't the end. Eight months later, in February 2026, Nissan filed two more recalls. The first one (26V-080) covered 323,917 Rogues and pinned the blame on heat and the oil itself degrading under high running temperatures. NHTSA's filing warns the consequences can go beyond a stalled engine, noting "a bearing failure may cause a breach in the engine block, allowing hot oil to be discharged, increasing the risk of an engine fire." The second recall (26V-081) covered 318,781 Rogues for a gear inside the electronic throttle body that can fracture during startup. Across the three campaigns, Nissan has recalled more than a million VC-Turbo vehicles, though the two 2026 recalls overlap with some vehicles already covered by the 2025 campaign.

Owners have also complained about the VC-Turbo. One 2022 Rogue owner wrote on CarComplaints, where the VC-Turbo is rated "Pretty Bad," said that the dealer told them, "The engine is completely shot and needs to be replaced. Total cost $14000." Enthusiasts have soured on it as well over the years. According to Endurance Warranty, mechanics warn about ticking or knocking noises, which could indicate worn bearings and cost more than $5,000 in out-of-warranty repairs for VC-Turbo-equipped Rogues and Altimas.

We've previously covered Nissan's reliability, citing Consumer Reports, pointing to "ongoing issues with the clever but problematic variable-compression VC-Turbo engine" as one of the factors pushing Nissan down to eighth place among the most reliable used-car brands.

The hybrid Jeep 2.0-liter turbo-four didn't fail because of a design flaw; it failed because sand does not mix well with engine internals. NHTSA's filing for the November 2025 recall (25V-766) covered 112,859 of these PHEV SUVs after Chrysler identified a supplier quality lapse: the debris from the engine-block sand-casting process was never fully removed before the blocks went into production.

Left inside, that sand works its way through the engine and can eventually cause a fire or a dead engine. Chrysler didn't have a fix at the time of the recall and only started offering software updates and, where needed, engine block replacements in May 2026. These same 4xe hybrids had already been recalled once before over a separate battery fire risk.

Chrysler's 2.0-liter PHEV has stumbled before that, too. A 2022 recall (22V-865) included 62,909 Wrangler 4xe models over the engine just shutting down. The vehicle's own diagnostics can misread a communication fault and decide to just power off the vehicle while driving. This has led to two accidents and one injury. RepairPal also ranks the Wrangler 25th out of 26 compact SUVs when it comes to reliability, though that rating covers the whole lineup, not just the 4xe.

What's even worse is that the same problem resurfaced three years later, this time in the Grand Cherokee. The September 2025 recall (25V-576) covered 91,787 more PHEVs after Chrysler traced another defect to the hybrid control processor, which is a very similar problem description to the 2022 recall, just on a different model. One JL Wrangler Forums member said oil dilution had their 4xe asking for an oil change after under 310 miles. And if the engine goes bang, one owner got quoted $7,500 for a replacement 2.0T from the dealer.

Back in 1971, Chevy rushed the Vega's development into just 24 months to hit a deadline set by GM president Ed Cole. To save weight, engineers skipped the cylinder sleeves that a block like this would normally need. Instead, they bet on a hardened Reynolds Aluminum alloy carrying enough silicon to serve as the bore surface on its own, bolted to a conventional cast-iron head. It held up under normal use, but severe heat degraded that silicon content, and the pistons would then scuff against the weakened bore walls.

Aluminum and iron don't handle heat the same way, either, and that mismatch is what finally cracked the head gasket. Chevrolet made the problem worse — early Vegas shipped with a radiator too small for the engine's needs and no way to recover coolant once lost. Cracking valve stem seals let oil into the cylinders too, and since oil also carries heat away from the engine, that only makes overheating worse.

The car's other systems fared no better. In April 1972, Chevrolet recalled roughly 129,000 Vegas (72V075000) after backfires ruptured the muffler and ignited leaking gasoline. Less than two months later, another recall (72V112000) covered 350,000 more Vegas whose idle-stop solenoid bracket could jam the throttle open. Enthusiasts were also very critical, as one Ford-Trucks forum member described the original Vega in a thread on the worst GM engines: "You didn't change the oil every 3,000 miles. You replaced the block."

By 1974, overheating had become bad enough that Chevy notified 1.3 million owners it would cover damage under warranty. A real fix didn't come until 1976's "Dura-Built 140" engine — new long-life valve stem seals, and hydraulic valve lifters, a beefed-up head gasket, and new cooling passages for the engine. Chevy even covered it with a massive five-year/60,000-mile warranty.

#5651. 313 kW Rooftop Solar System at Virginia Elementary Will Save $581,000 in Energy Costs

Roanoke City Schools to Add 313 kW Solar Power System

Staunton, VA — Secure Solar Futures, a provider of on-site clean energy to schools, local governments, and businesses, will build a 313-kilowatt solar power system installed at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, VA. Construction of the system is expected later this year at no capital cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement with Secure Solar Futures. Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, a subsidiary of Pardee Resources Company, will provide the majority of the capital for the solar system.

A total of 531 bi-facial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, TX, will be installed on the rooftop of the school located at 3142 Preston Avenue, NW, and will offset 67% of the power used by the school annually.

In its first year, the school’s solar system will produce 421 megawatt hours of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes and provide environmental benefits by avoiding 371 metric tons of carbon pollution, which is equal to the emissions produced by 87 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, or the carbon sequestered by 372 acres of U.S. forests, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Under the Power Purchase Agreement, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, together with its partner Secure Solar Futures, will own, operate, and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

During the term of the Power Purchase Agreement, Preston Park Elementary School will save $581,000 in net avoided costs for electricity. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s 35- to 40-year productive lifespan.

Roanoke City Public Schools (RCPS) is an urban school division in Roanoke, Virginia, serving a pre-K through 12th grade population of approximately 14,000 students. RCPS provides an inclusive and equitable, student-centered culture that empowers lifelong learning. Through meaningful, relevant, and engaging learning opportunities, we will empower all students to dream, excel, and meet their full potential to benefit our city and its citizens. The division has 17 elementary schools, five middle schools, two high schools, and five program locations, including the Roanoke Valley Governor’s School for Science & Technology and two career and technical education centers. Visit www.rcps.info for additional information.

#5650. 7 Fuel Sipping Classic Cars For Thrifty Driving Enthusiasts

It might seem anachronistic to chase fuel economy when you're hunting for a classic car. But it's not absurd to want an affordable classic if that's all your wallet can muster. And in that case, it's probably also true that you're hardly itching to shell out for a massive weekly thrashing at the pump. After all, however you define a classic, they tend to be parts-and-labor-costs hungry. At the time of this writing, AAA says the national average for a gallon of gas sits at $4.12, up 36% versus a year ago, when it was $3.04. And in California a gallon of regular will run you $5.87. Ouch.

Plus you've got a pocket humblebrag at the ready wherever you cruise in your fuel-sipping steed. Imagine showing up at a cars and coffee with your vintage ride and telling the assembled dudes (always, always, dudes) that your 1990 Honda CRX gets a combined 40-ish mpg  – which torches the fuel economy of most modern cars.

Even if you're not solely chasing fuel economy, you can be frugal and have fun simultaneously. Take, for instance, a merely 23-year-old Mini Cooper S. It gets 31 mpg on the highway and its supercharged 1.6-liter engine can tug you to 60 mph in 6.9 seconds. That's not too shabby for a car that Hagerty valuation puts at somewhere between $8,000 and $11,000. It's pretty tough to name another used city ripper that lean on gas and as entertaining to drive.

Well, actually, I'll try. Since the whole reason for this game is to induce debate among Jalopnik readers who live to lambaste our dumb lists.

The Honda CRX, according to Hagerty, has skyrocketed in value, up over 113% in the past three years. Now you'll pay at least $14,000 for one. That said, what soulless used car might you get instead for that kind of money?

Plus, the CRX (in the HF "High Fuel" version) delivered up to 47 mpg! Even models with reasonably higher output, like the 91-horsepower 1.5Si, breached the 30 mpg mark. Possibly the reason the CRX has risen in collectors' eyes has to do with the simple idea that a car that weighs less than 2,000 pounds doesn't need more than 91 horsepower. And in the guise of the 1.5Si, a contemporary review in Car & Driver found the sport suspension ideal for twisty corners, and at 1,840 pounds, 91 horsepower was more than adequate. Yeah, every CRX should have featured two engines, but I'm guessing that'd be bad for fuel economy and the concept of this list.

If you're hunting, from 1988 onward the CRX got four-wheel double-wishbone suspension and ditched the less advanced torsion-bar front and beam-axle rear of older CRXs. By 1990, Honda had added four-wheel disc brakes to the Si grade.

These lithe two-doors feature a funky non-second row, with a bench behind the front seats that can be flipped down to yield a reasonably capacious hatch space. That makes the CRX a more pragmatic sporty car than, say, the Fiat X 1/9 on this list.

If you're pursuing a classic that's fuel-sipping, you probably don't want to spend a fortune to acquire it. That's kind of defeating the point. Toyota's mid-engine MR2, which we got in many guises in the U.S. from 1985 through the early 2000s, has a strong following. Maybe too strong. Hagerty says turbocharged 200-horsepower W20s — the second-generation MR2 with softer shoulders and a longer wheelbase — run between $23,000 and nearly $39,000.

Okay, those are faster. But at that price they're blowing a huge hole in this story's premise. Of course, the reason you want one is the same reason you might lust after the Fiat X 1/9 on this list. When they're properly engineered, mid-engine cars can offer magical balance through corners; Hagerty called this first generation, the W10, "flickable."

That's the joy you're after, and you can also still afford the W10, which averages from $10,300 to $18,000 per Hagerty. These were only good for 112 hp from a tiny 1.6-liter inline-4. But that still meant you could gallop to 60 mph in 8.2 seconds according to Car & Driver — and that version of the MR2 achieved 27 mpg in the city.

Want more oomph? One route is the middle-ground supercharged W10 MR2, which won't hurt you too much at the pump, delivering 23 mpg city and 28 highway. Output jumped to 145 hp, resulting in a 6.5-second 0-60 sprint. Hagerty says these range between $15,800 and $26,200, which isn't that harsh a price penalty, and still cheaper than later W20s.

Not that you need my two cents, since scads of automotive journalists have owned or currently own 1990s MX-5 Miatas, but in my experience this car absolutely fits the remit of both frugality and fun. Also, I stand firmly with the crowd that says everyone should drive a Miata at least once. I frequently loathe the fact I sold mine. It was a trouble-free grin machine.

Okay, they're slow, too. With a 116-hp 1.6-liter inline-4 you're not going to win many stoplight wars. But that's not what matters. The early 1990s MX-5 Miata, at 155 inches long (a scant 13 feet), is nearly 2 feet shorter than a current Porsche 911 Carrera. Pint-sized and low in weight — barely 2,200 pounds — makes carving around corners gloriously entertaining. To me, the Miata is one of very few cars that's fantastically entertaining even when you're driving slower than the speed limit.

Hagerty says finding a Miata from the early 1990s ought to run you between about $7,000 and $12,200, and with a combined fuel economy of 24 mpg, these little five-speeds are reasonably economical to operate, if not exactly trying to swipe that Honda CRX's crown. Miatas are also considered highly reliable, which is another measure of thrift. And that's in contrast to the British two-seat sports cars of the 1960s and 1970s they were designed to copy.

The 1979 Fiat X 1/9 is neither as logical as the Honda CRX nor as practical. It's here because it achieved 26 mpg city fuel economy and because we think the "driving enthusiasts" of our headline find going around corners more fun than bombing straight ahead.

Besides, with only 67 horsepower from its 1.5-liter engine, the Fiat X 1/9 wasn't designed with the quarter mile in mind. Instead, with its mid-engine, rear-wheel-drive setup, the Fiat puts all its mass (plus, you, the driver) in the middle of the machine. Car & Driver argued that made the Fiat a blast for scorching around corners, and yet kind enough to less seasoned drivers. Meaning, it loses grip progressively, rather than suddenly, so it's less likely to cause you physical harm.

The magazine also found that it took nearly 12 seconds to journey to 60 mph, so if you're hurt behind the wheel of the  X 1/9, it might be because other drivers have grown impatient in your wake. Then again, just let them pass! You're cruising under sunshine thanks to the Fiat's removable lightweight lid that can be stowed quickly in the front trunk.

This Fiat is definitely emblematic of la dolce vita. Also, it's a pretty affordable, sweet way to motor, since Hagerty ballparks a 1979 X 1/9 between $8,600 and $14,000. That's not the $7,115 Car & Driver said this model cost when tested. But adjusted for inflation, that 1979 cash would be worth $35,100 today, so your $8,600 X 1/9 is a dang bargain.

Acura Integras from the late 1990s are no longer sleepers. Hagerty puts the high end of the 1997 Acura Integra Type R at north of $50,000. Is that expensive or cheap? The brand-new 320-horsepower Integra Type S costs about that much. Keeping budget constraints top of mind here, the Type R is a no-go. But the still-quick Integra GS-R averages more like $10,000 to $20,000 if you eyeball recent sales on Bring a Trailer. For instance, in September 2026, a 2000 Integra GS-R sold there for $20,750.

That's still a car that brings the noise to the tune of 170 hp and an 8,100 rpm redline. My dad had one and I adored that car; he gave me the family Toyota Tercel instead. Woot.

Putting my nostalgia aside, a 1994 Car & Driver shootout of hot hatches awarded the GS-R its top prize in large part for its blend of motorcycle-like revs, excellent five-speed gearbox, and the car's predictable, capable, rewarding handling. Also, its 1.8-liter inline-4 is loud as hell when you're deep in the throttle, which makes the Integra seem properly exotic. Yet, drive it sanely and it's hardly deafening.

Is the Integra the most economical car here? Hardly. Its combined fuel economy of 24 mpg is just decent. Still, you're getting a hatchback that's cheaper on gas than lots of vintage muscle iron, and if you can find one around $20,000 you'll be spending less than the price of any new sports car. You might also care that the Integra even has a functional backseat and decent luggage space.

By 1989, Mercedes-Benz was making very hot versions of the 190, which began production in 1982. For instance, a 1989 Mercedes-Benz 190E 2.5-16 Evolution, one of only 502 produced, was bid up to nearly $100,000 on Bring a Trailer this spring. Neat. But that hardly fits the mandate of frugality.

The W120/190 series Benz you probably want would be the modest 72-horsepower 2.2-liter mid-1980s diesel, if in fact your goal is long-wearing life and relatively strong 30 mpg combined fuel economy. Oh, and also unlike a Cosworth-hotted-up 190 that's ticking boxes for collectors capable of throwing down 100 grand, Hagerty puts the price of a used 190D with a base 2.2-liter diesel at as cheap as $3,500.

You could spend a little more and get a modest power bump to the later 1980s 2.5-liter diesel with 93 horsepower, which still delivers 28 mpg combined, and Hagerty says will cost you between $4,067 and $7,367. Again, name any modern car you can find for so little money.

All right, I know this is the least enthusiast-focused car in this compilation. But Mercedes gifted the 190 with a five-link rear suspension and gas-filled struts up front, and that yielded if not a purely sporty vibe, a very confident, modern and comfortable ride. You're buying one because they're cheap to acquire, drink diesel slowly, and like a lot of vintage Benzes, are solid as tanks.

Last year we told you the 2025 Mini Cooper S 4 Door is like a half-trained puppy you love with all your heart. The thing is, that car's 2026 base price (even without optional paddle shifters) is $34,150 including destination. And there's no option to get a stick-shift version. You may argue that it's a new car, and with 201 horsepower will walk all over a 20-year-old version of the supercharged Mini Cooper S. Sure thing. But that 168-hp supercharged 1.5-liter inline 4 had more character than the turbocharged 2.0-liter in the new car.

No, that didn't make it quick. Its 0-60 mph times ran about 6.9 seconds, while the new one takes 6.3 seconds. Seriously, do you want to pay nearly $30,000 more for a new Mini Cooper S that's less than a second faster to 60 mph, when a 2005 just sold for $4,000 on Bring a Trailer?

There's a Cooper S in my extended family, so I get to drive one pretty regularly. It needs some work. All old cars do. But this one has north of 200,000 miles and it's still ripping around. Just remember to find one with the fun six-speed when you look for your O.G. Mini Cooper S R53, and avoid the version with the continuously variable automatic transmission. Our Mini Cooper burns a little oil, roughly half a quart every three months, which isn't a big deal, and the EPA combined average fuel economy of 25 mpg is spot on.

Today, this counts as a small car, but it's big enough to be useful, with flip-down rear seats and enough gumption to keep up on the interstate. Fun, frugal, and just old enough to have loads of character? Check, check, and check.

#5649. Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas

Fossil fuels are slowly beginning to lose their grip on the global transportation sector, with one key omission: rocket fuel. The rocket fuel conundrum has earned an uptick in attention in recent years, now that rocket launches, once rare, are becoming as commonplace as rush hour traffic. The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

With its future volume of launch operations in mind, SpaceX aims to exercise as much control as possible over its fuel supply. The company is investing in its own natural gas pipelines and on-site fuel production facilities to help ensure that the taps don’t run dry, though it still relies on the gas industry to find the stuff and bring it up from the ground.

SpaceX has already been sucking up a copious amount of natural gas for its existing operations in Texas and Florida. “SpaceX (SPCX) is emerging as one of the largest new customers for natural gas,” reported the oil and gas analytics firm East Daley in October.

“Unlike Falcon 9, which burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, Starship creates a direct link between launch activity and natural gas consumption. SPCX plans to process and liquefy pipeline gas into liquid methane to fuel the rockets,” East Daley elaborates.

As described by East Daley, the SpaceX subsidiary Coastal Connect Services is planning a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline to hook up SpaceX operations in Cape Canaveral, Florida with existing infrastructure jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer.

Meanwhile, at the company’s launch site and newly incorporated (as of 2025) City of Starbase in Cameron County, Texas, plans are in motion for SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development to connect the new 8-mile “Starpipe” natural gas pipeline with another 145-mile pipeline currently being built by the firms WhiteWater, Enbridge, and MPLX. Starpipe is expected to begin shuttling natural gas into Starbase Texas early next year.

The two pipeline projects come alongside word that SpaceX has nailed down approvals for parts of a new $100 billion project that expands the company’s US footprint into another combination city-and-launch-site under the name of Starbase, Louisiana. The new city will presumably also require a reliable supply of natural gas for on-site rocket fuel production.

For the record, Starbase, Louisiana is not part of the educational non-profit organization STARBASE Louisiana, an affiliate of the national STARBASE program of the US Department of Defense, aimed at stimulating interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) topics among 5th grade students. The Louisiana branch of STARBASE is located Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier Parish, in the northwestern part of the state.

Starbase, Louisiana will take up 125,000 acres of land at Pecan Island in a marshy region along the southern coast in Vermilion Parish, where plans are being laid for 30 launches per day. More than a dozen launch towers will eventually sprout up at the site, where the operation will include producing rocket fuel.

If you’ve gotten wind of the project under the name “Osprey,” you’re not dreaming. The new city was reportedly code-named “Project Osprey” during initial discussions with public officials. As described by the Gulf State News affiliate WWNO (New Orleans Public Radio) on November 11, Project Osprey was shrouded in secrecy during the initial negotionas, with “dozens” of local officials signing non-disclosure agreements that limited what they could say about the project.

The Osprey code name also reportedly enabled Vermilion Parish officials to sidestep public participation in ostensibly public hearings on the Starbase, Louisiana project earlier this year. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry finally let the cat out of the bag in a public announcement in August. Local residents and the nonprofit organization Vermillion Citizens coalition have already filed a lawsuit against the project, alleging that parish officials approved parts of Starbase, Louisiana in violation of the state’s Open Public Meetings Law.

If and when shovels hit the ground on Starbase, Louisiana, the Trump administration is taking steps to help ensure that natural gas producers in the US come through with the goods — not just for SpaceX, of course, although the firm has become a market-mover in the gas industry as noted by East Daley.

On November 10, for example, the US Department of Energy announced the finishing touches on a $480 million loan in support of Project Elkhorn, an endeavor under the umbrella of the oil and gas firm Arena Energy. Project Elkhorn covers the modernization of 22 existing platforms off the Louisiana coast — coincidentally or not, the same state that expects to host the new Starbase city.

Arena launched in 1999 with a focus on revitalizing mature oil and gas fields. According to the Energy Department, Project Elkhorn will ramp natural gas production up to 77 million cubic feet per day at peak production among the 22 platforms, alongside up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day. By way of contrast, the 22 platforms currently produce 30,000 barrels of oil per day. Over the lifespan of Project Elkhorn, the collective total is expected to add 25 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to the US fossil energy roster.

As CEO of the leading EV maker Tesla, Elon Musk has earned his share of credit for rescuing electric cars from the dustbin of automotive obscurity and vaulting them into the mainstream mobility market of today — if not so much here in the US, then certainly overseas. Musk’s other ventures, on the other hand, threaten to offset, if not override, whatever sustainability gains are to be made from EVs.

In addition to SpaceX, Musk’s xAI data centers have also contributed to spiking demand for natural gas. Last year word dropped that Musk’s Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee trucked in approximately three dozen industrial-sized gas generators to power the site, at least 15 of which were already in operation without an air quality permit. The Southern Environmental Law Center has been among those raising the alarm over toxic emissions from the generators, which lack the pollution controls required of permanent power plants.

Natural gas also factors into a new data center planned for the SpaceX-backed City of Starbase, Texas, which sits adjacent to Brownsville. The city of Brownsville recently imposed a temporary moratorium on new data center construction. According to ABC News affiliate KVUE and other sources, earlier this year Elon Musk asked Brownsville officials to de-annex a parcel of land at its outskirts, evidently in order to building a $24 billion data center at the site along with a new gas-fired power plant for a new data center to be located in Starbase. The request was granted, enabling the project to skirt around the Brownsville moratorium.

Starbase city officials are scheduled to conduct a public hearing on the new data center on December 9, where presumably they will decide whether or not the project can make due with gas generators until a full gas power plant with appropriate pollution controls can materialize.

Over and above the rocket fuel issue, grassroots activists, environmental organizations, and researchers have been raising the alarm over the impact of Starbase in Texas for years, tracking significant harm to local public recreation resources as well as wildlife habitats. Similar concerns have surfaced around SpaceX’s plans for Starbase, Louisiana.

Of course, nobody seriously expects the whole domestic rocket business to stop in its tracks. The issue is one of mitigating climate and biodiversity risks, developing projects that avoid pummeling vulnerable communities with additional public health risks, and investing in more sustainable options including alternative rocket fuels.

Keep an eye on the aviation industry for some hints at the future of sustainable propellants. Airline stakeholders have been focusing on SAF, generally meaning a bio-based equivalent of kerosene jet fuel. However, the going has been slow, and it’s even slower in the field of propellants. The European Space Agency, for example, has been exploring green propellants for space operations for 25 years, with little to show for its efforts.

More recently, though, aviation stakeholders have begun turning to the emerging electrofuels or “solar fuels” industry, meaning fuels synthesized from captured carbon and green hydrogen, with solar and other renewables powering the operation. The green hydrogen industry has been struggling for traction, but signs of scaleup have finally emerged, with e-kerosene jet fuel in play along with green hydrogen. Honda, for one, is envisioning a fleet of reusable rockets propelled by renewable fuels, and at least two Chinese firms are also working the reusable rocket angle.

Image: SpaceX is among the industrial-scale consumers of natural gas adding more pipes to the nation’s sprawling network of gas pipelines, which the startup needs to ensure a steady supply of fuel for its growing fleet of rockets (courtesy of US Energy Information Agency).

Tina has been covering advanced energy technology, military sustainability, emerging materials, biofuels, ESG and related policy and political matters for CleanTechnica since 2009. Follow her @tinamcasey on LinkedIn, Mastodon or Bluesky.

#5648. Major Change to Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines

— ACS now recommends PSA testing every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69

Shifting gears on prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69.

Since the release of its previous guideline 16 years ago, the ACS had recommended that average-risk men consult with a physician before deciding for themselves whether to undergo a screening PSA test.

The new ACS recommendations also strengthened guidelines for men at high risk for prostate cancer, recommending annual screening beginning at age 45 for Black men and those with a strong family history of the disease. The organization previously recommended that those men discuss the pros and cons of screening with a physician at age 40 or 45.

The changes reflect the accumulation of stronger evidence that screening PSA tests reduce prostate cancer mortality and diagnosis of late-stage disease, according to the updated guidelines from Robert Smith, PhD, ACS senior vice president for early cancer detection science, and colleagues, appearing in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians.

"We've just reached a point in our understanding of prostate cancer, especially that [screening] can reduce the risk of being diagnosed with metastatic disease and dying of prostate cancer," Smith told MedPage Today. "We have good protocols for avoiding harms."

Smith noted that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not updated their prostate cancer screening guidelines since 2018. For average-risk men, the USPSTF recommends discussion-backed decisions on PSA testing for men ages 55 to 69.

"I cannot tell you what [their recommendations] would be if they updated them today, but they did not have the data in 2018 that we had in 2025 with the update of the European trial data showing the endurance of the mortality reduction," said Smith.

The update aligns with recent evidence supporting PSA screening for prostate cancer as "one of the most important steps men can take to protect their health," said Ash Tewari, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"We have strong evidence that PSA testing can reduce the risk of dying from prostate cancer, and advances in MRI and other diagnostic tools are helping us identify potentially dangerous cancers while avoiding unnecessary procedures," he said. "Knowing your risk, getting screened regularly, and having these conversations early can save lives."

With the update, the ACS takes a clear position on prostate cancer screening, said Mark Ashamalla, MD, of Episcopal Health Services in New York City.

"For years, the ACS largely focused on encouraging men to discuss the pros and cons of PSA screening with their doctors," said Ashamalla. "Now they're taking a much clearer position and actually recommending regular screening. For men at average risk, that means a PSA blood test every 2 years between ages 50 and 69, while Black men and those with a strong family history should begin annual screening at age 45. This is a significant shift and reflects growing evidence that regular screening can reduce the risk of advanced prostate cancer and save lives."

"The goal isn't to find and treat every prostate cancer," he added. "It's to catch the dangerous ones early enough to make a difference. I think that's the biggest takeaway from these new guidelines."

By way of the guidelines, the ACS also recommends:

The updated guidelines are supportive of the recent trend toward active surveillance as the primary option for men with low-risk prostate cancer.

"It's important to recognize that prostate cancer screening has evolved over the past 30 years," said Smith. "More and more people appreciate that very worrisome harms associated with therapy can be avoided, especially if a man is diagnosed with prostate cancer that is not aggressive. Active treatment should be avoided until such time as it appears that the disease has become aggressive. Some men may be diagnosed with a prostate cancer that's not very aggressive, and they will live with it in that state for the rest of their lives. [They can] avoid harms that are quite diminishing to quality of life."

"On the other hand, if a man's prostate cancer becomes more aggressive, and treatment is necessary, then the process of active surveillance will at least have postponed it for a number of years, allowing men to not have to live with those [treatment-related] side effects," said Smith.

#5647. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#5646. Sonnen, SOLRITE, & ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets

SOLRITE Unveils Next-Gen Virtual Power Plant Node with sonnen and ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets

ADAPT Energy’s control of VPP breakers will add dispatchable load flexibility to the SOLRITE sonnen VPP, while paving a simpler, faster, and lower-cost path to whole-home backup

SOLRITE, a company specializing in developing, financing, and owning Virtual Power Plant Agreement (VPA) projects, together with Sonnen, a leader in Virtual Power Plant energy storage technology, announced they will now digitally integrate VPP smart breakers, managed by ADAPT Energy, into the SOLRITE  sonnen VPP. The integration marks the next evolution of sonnen and SOLRITE’s industry-leading partnership in VPP innovation, expanding beyond battery storage by transforming residential electrical loads into flexible, dispatchable grid assets for both the VPP and smart backup power applications.

Unlike traditional approaches to whole-home backup, often requiring hard-wired circuit relocation, including exclusive loads panels, the newly expanded VPP Node combines the sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to intelligently manage major household loads. This creates a more streamlined approach to whole-home backup while unlocking an entirely new source of flexibility for the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. With homeowner permission, the VPP smart breaker—controlled by ADAPT Energy—can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be flexible for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and Founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The integration addresses one of the longstanding challenges of whole-home backup: how to provide broad electrical coverage without having large household loads drain available battery capacity too quickly or cause the nano-grid to immediately fail after an off-grid transition due to excessive inrush current. With the newly expanded VPP smart breaker technology digitally integrated with the sonnen ecosystem, the system can intelligently shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns. This significantly reduces installation complexity and tedious inspections for installers, allowing crews to complete more jobs per week.

For homeowners, the system provides the convenience of a whole-home electrical configuration that intelligently manages the loads that have the greatest impact on backup duration. This work is all done in the background, meaning homeowners do not have to worry about resetting individual circuits during an outage. Instead, participating homes will see more value from their VPA program in the form of an enhanced backup power experience. Furthermore, at any time in the future, if a homeowner is interested in altering which of their VPP smart breaker-controlled loads are shed during an outage, the process to make such a change is quick and easy, requiring no electrical reconfiguration.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, President of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

The permission-based architecture aligns the interests of the homeowner, battery owner and utility. The real opportunity comes when homeowners choose to opt in to allow the breakers to participate in on-grid VPP events.

When a VPP event is dispatched, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge in concert with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads, and by using Eaton AbleEdge breakers, ADAPT achieves this right where the breaker sits, without relocation. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid. That way, the VPP can respond through both energy stored in the battery and energy that would have otherwise been consumed by the home, thereby increasing the dispatched injection into the grid, by the VPP.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, Chairman and CEO of sonnen Inc. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”
