#5570. Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency

Industry Voices—From pledges to progress: Kill the clipboard, keep an eye on consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

For many patients, the clipboard remains one of healthcare’s most familiar frustrations.

At nearly every visit, patients are asked to provide information they have already supplied elsewhere, including their insurance coverage, medications, family history and previous surgeries. This repetitious hassle—even if managed on tablets as in recent years—frustrates patients, increases the risk of incomplete or inaccurate information entering the record, and takes unnecessary staff time to reconcile.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ Health Technology Ecosystem initiative offers a compelling alternative through the Kill the Clipboard pledge. The effort is focused on moving technology and care practices forward so that patients can more easily retrieve and share their health information through personal health records or other health apps, removing the need for their data to be reconstructed at every encounter.

That shift could conclusively improve the patient experience. Reaching that goal, however, will require more than voluntary commitments from individual technology developers. This multi-stakeholder initiative needs work based on consensus-based standards, reliable infrastructure, clear data governance and careful attention to how new capabilities affect clinical work.

Patients often assume that health data interoperability is happening more than it is, and certainly more easily. In some cases, a person opens an app and shares their information with a provider themselves; in others, the exchange is initiated by their clinical care team. Behind that process, though, is a complex chain of care organizations, electronic health records (EHRs), identity verification services, intermediaries, standards development organizations, application developers and networks.

Consider, for example, real-time prescription benefit information. Giving patients cost and coverage options during an encounter—and ensuring that the information is accurate all the way to the point of sale—could help increase affordability and medication adherence. Yet the experience depends on pharmacy networks, price comparison apps and other third parties delivering complete, timely information into the clinician’s prescribing workflow, all while the patient is there in the exam room or awaiting discharge from the hospital. Every participant in the chain is fundamental to the increasingly complex web of health information exchange.

A 2025 study of more than 8,100 family physicians published in JAMA Network Open underscores just how much work around data-sharing remains. Depending on the type of clinical information, only 8% to 19% of survey respondents reported that outside data were routinely available, easy to find and easy to use within their EHRs.

Pledges like Kill the Clipboard can establish a valuable direction for the industry and encourage momentum. They will face challenges with adoption and impact, however, if sufficient effort doesn’t go into resolving dependencies across the country’s health tech ecosystem. Clear technical standards, realistic implementation timelines and ways to verify that promised capabilities work in practice are essential.

While the goals of increasing patient control over their own data, tackling inefficiencies, and increasing affordable care delivery are laudable and things no one would argue with, it is also true that moving quickly without those foundations could create expensive rework down the road or inadvertently widen the digital divide. If any or all pledge criteria eventually become certification requirements, as Dr. Tom Keane, the National Coordinator for Health IT, has intimated could be a possibility, the variability in readiness among different companies could become a problematic gap.

Expanding digital access also raises important questions about how patient data will be used once it leaves a regulated clinical environment.

There has been a huge proliferation of health apps in recent years intended to help patients more actively manage their own health while also better managing their medical records. Many can deliver meaningful value, but patients who are considering use of such an app need clearer information about whether an application may retain, combine, share or sell their data. Consent language should be understandable, with governance expectations following the information across the digital ecosystem, but the current legal and regulatory system needs modernization to ensure sufficient patient awareness.

Patient matching presents another safety concern. A larger volume of exchanged data is useful only when organizations can confidently connect each record to the correct person. Striking the right balance between the stringency of matching criteria and the goal of increasing data exchange is critical, as a clinician could make a prescribing or treatment decision based on another person’s medications, allergies, diagnoses or laboratory results with damaging consequences. Strong identity verification and thoughtful matching practices therefore belong at the center of any effort to make health data more portable, ensuring that patient safety protections are inherent to the matching process.

The potential consequences have recently been measured. A 2026 BMJ Quality & Safety study found that hospitalized patients with duplicate charts had 3.5 times the odds of requiring intensive care, 4.7 times the odds of inpatient death and hospital stays that were 32% longer than those of matched patients without duplicate charts. Although the observational study does not establish causation, it underscores the clinical risks associated with fragmented patient information.

For virtually any initiative focused on the patient, program vision and software design must also account for the people delivering care.

Primary care clinicians often have only a few minutes to review a patient’s record, conduct their initial assessment of the problem, complete documentation of the encounter, place orders and determine any necessary follow-up. While unquestionably helpful, adding review of new extensive patient data that has been sent from a patient’s medical record aggregation app adds another step that takes time. Then, needing to build in time to consider prescription cost comparisons, scheduling stemming from referrals, discussions of patient consent preferences, or record reconciliation further consumes part of a tightly constrained visit.

The impact on the provider and staff workflows in no way diminishes the value to the patient. These changes benefit all of us as patients and/or caregivers ourselves—but the implications for that workflow cannot be an afterthought.

The strongest implementations will embed new capabilities directly into existing workflows and surface information exactly when it is most useful. Software developers should also involve practicing clinicians in design, testing and governance so that any improvements support better care without introducing avoidable friction. In fact, prioritizing the efficient implementation of these new functionalities will increase adoption and user satisfaction, moving us all closer to our collective goals.

Eliminating the clipboard is the correct ambition, as are the goals of the other Health Tech Ecosystem pledges. They would serve patients nationwide and represent broader industry change in how we move and manage information. Patients should not have to recount their histories every time they seek care, and clinicians should have dependable data available whenever decisions must be made.

With mature standards, real-time connectivity, responsible governance, reliable patient matching and thoughtful workflow design, we can collectively turn the pledge’s aims into a new reality: more trusted digital experiences that give patients greater control and help everyone involved in their care act with greater confidence.

Leigh Burchell is vice president of policy and public affairs at Altera Digital Health, as well as chair of the Electronic Health Record Association.

#5567. The Fine Print on Our National Bet

— As online sports betting becomes routine, its mental health costs are becoming harder to dismiss

Nothing is more absurd than a direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical commercial, or an online sports betting commercial.

At least the pharmaceutical ad has the decency to be honest about its absurdity. A smiling couple strolls along a beach as a voice-over races through a pharmacologic inventory of calamity: nausea, insomnia, rash, suicidal thoughts, spontaneous combustion -- well, perhaps not that last one, but give the announcer time. Across the bottom of the screen, safety information scrolls at the speed of a stock ticker during a market crash. The viewer is left with a vague sense that the medication may cure a minor inconvenience while replacing it with several more interesting problems.

Sports-betting commercials have adopted the same visual grammar, with a stranger moral logic. The smiling young men on screen aren't walking on a beach; they are shouting at televisions, tapping phones, and celebrating a three-point shot as if they had personally discovered penicillin. Then, below the spectacle: "If you or someone you know has a gambling problem, call the National Problem Gambling Helpline."

It is the public health equivalent of putting a fire extinguisher on a flamethrower and calling it responsible.

The disclaimer acknowledges what the advertisement otherwise works hard to conceal: sports gambling is not merely entertainment. It is a commercial product designed to encourage repeated use, normalize risk, and convert attention into revenue. The app is in the pocket. The odds are refreshed constantly. The promotion is personalized. The game no longer ends when the final whistle blows because there is always another game, another parlay, another "risk-free" offer that is neither risk-free nor especially free.

We have taken an activity once associated with casinos, racetracks, and back rooms and made it as frictionless as ordering dinner. Then we seem surprised that some people order too much.

A recent JAMA Psychiatry study adds empirical support to what clinicians have observed in less formal settings. The authors found that legalization of online sports betting was associated with increases in the probability of antidepressant and anti-anxiety medication use, as well as increased outpatient visits for depression and anxiety among adults with employer-sponsored insurance.

Most people who bet on football will not need psychotherapy. But why have we built a system that increases exposure to a potentially addictive activity, then treats the resulting distress as an unfortunate side effect rather than a predictable cost of doing business? The answer, of course, is money. It is almost always money, dressed in a blazer and labeled innovation.

Sports leagues, media companies, betting platforms, and states profit from tax revenues. Influencers profit from sponsorships, affiliate links, paid subscriptions, and online engagement when they market supposedly certain betting picks as "locks," even when their followers lose money on those bets. Meanwhile, the gambler absorbs the losses, and families may absorb the debt, secrecy, conflict, and despair. Clinicians and behavioral health systems absorb the aftermath. This arrangement is often sold as individual freedom, a useful phrase whenever someone else is making the money.

This type of "freedom" is not unique to gambling. Debates over cannabis legalization, drug decriminalization, alcohol policy, tobacco, and other forms of consumption repeatedly reveal the same ethical tension. However, legalizing or decriminalizing illicit drugs does not reduce overall use; in many cases, it is associated with increased consumption or with use that remains relatively stable, depending on the substance and region. The relevant question is not simply, "Should this be legal?" It is, "What system of incentives are we creating, and who bears the consequences?"

Government often acts as though revenue is a moral anesthetic. People describe gambling tax proceeds, whether from betting or the lottery, as funding for schools, roads, or public services, as if the money's destination negates the circumstances of its collection. A dollar is a dollar, except when it is earned through the slow accumulation of losses among people least able to afford them. We would do well to ask whether a state budget should rely, even in part, on gambling-tax revenue when that revenue depends on bettors losing money.

Elected officials like revenue, voters like convenience, and professional sports has become an entertainment-industrial complex that is too large, too beloved, and too well sponsored to criticize without seeming humorless. Nobody wants to be the person who interrupts the playoff party to ask whether the game has become a delivery system for gambling products.

But we can ask: What is the role of clinicians in a system that profits from predictable harm? Should we attack the entertainment-industrial complex as we once did the medical-industrial complex -- and lose? I don't think clinicians should become scolds, prohibitionists, or cultural referees. We should become witnesses. We see the patient who cannot sleep because of debt. We see the spouse who discovers hidden accounts. We see anxiety worsened by financial instability, depression complicated by shame, and crises that appear in the chart as insomnia, panic, alcohol misuse, or suicidal thinking rather than "sports betting." We recognize that an individual need not show up with a casino chip to prove they are addicted.

Our voices should be present in legislative hearings, hospital community-benefit plans, professional society statements, public health campaigns, and medical education. Screening for gambling-related harm should become more routine where clinically appropriate, especially when patients present with abrupt financial distress, escalating anxiety, depression, substance use, or relationship conflict. We should also insist that prevention not be outsourced to a phone number scrolling beneath a commercial that makes restraint look unfashionable.

The National Problem Gambling Helpline is necessary, but it should not serve as the ethical fig leaf for an industry that profits when people keep betting.

A society reveals its values not only by what it prohibits but also by what it promotes, subsidizes, glamorizes, and calls entertainment. If we are going to place a sportsbook on every smartphone, we should at least be honest about the wager. The house may not always win in the short term, but it has already convinced us to keep playing.

#5566. Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency

Patient experience has improved across the healthcare industry. Now comes consistency" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient experience metrics collected over millions of encounters show continuous topline improvements across all types of care settings, either meeting or surpassing those reported ahead of the pandemic.

But the gains aren’t uniform, with substantial variation between organizations, regions, patient groups, admission types, specialty and other operational factors under providers’ control, warned Qualtrics in its “State of Patient Experience 2026” report, released Thursday.

“The national trendline is encouraging, but tells an incomplete story,” the report reads. “Some organizations are improving rapidly; others are standing still.”

The experience management software vendor’s analysis, released Thursday, pulled data from 43.1 million of its over 2,500 hospitals and 490,000 medical office site customers.

It showed national patient experience scores like Likelihood to Recommend (LTR) reached new highs in ambulatory surgery (86 out of 100), medical practice (86), inpatient (70.5) and emergency department (69.5) settings through 2025. Overall ratings across each of those settings also improved from the prior year, with the exception of a slight decline (70.4 to 69.7) among inpatient facilities.

Several data points highlighted in the report paint the picture of how inconsistencies or other operational hurdles can impact patients’ reported experiences, and how providers with the best overall satisfaction scores stand out in those areas.

When comparing a planned versus an unplanned admission, for instance, hospitals in the top quartile of overall patient experience scores recorded an 8.9-point median gap between the two encounter types. At bottom-quartile hospitals, unplanned admissions were a median 18.2 points lower.

At the same time, practices that encourage consistent care delivery can make scores for unplanned visits look more like their counterparts. Here, the vendor pointed to bedside shifts, a nursing practice in which nurses going off duty update the on-duty nurse with patient care information at the bedside. A planned admission that did not have a bedside shift was tied to a 68.3 LTR, versus a 76.5 LTR during an unplanned admission that included a bedside shift.

That data point is also an example of the loyalty benefit providers can enjoy when implementing practices to address operational friction, described as a chief drag on patients’ likelihood to recommend a provider. In an inpatient setting, for instance, patients who reported no operational friction rewarded hospitals with LTR scores of 90.6, versus 60.3 when friction is present. These types of operational factors had a greater negative impact on experience scores than those related to clinical care, per Qualtrics’ data.

“The highest performing organizations double down on reliability and consistency, making exceptional experiences the standard, not the exception,” the report reads.

Another standout in the data was patients’ favorable responses to caregivers demonstrating teamwork and trust. Units in the top quartile for teamwork (where patients report “staff worked together for you”) were almost twice as likely to notch top hospital ratings, while those with high levels of trust (as reported by employees) are about 2.4 times as likely to be a top performer.

“Teamwork has emerged as the defining key driver of confidence in care and lasting loyalty,” the report reads. “Patients notice when caregivers communicate clearly, coordinate effectively, and work together toward a common goal.”

Qualtrics’ report concludes with several patient experience recommendations for organizations to target in the coming year. Among these are embracing omnichannel listening, or combining traditional metrics like survey data with other channels; reducing workforce administrative burden to maximize patient face time; and removing barriers that keep patients from making an appointment, including by reserving slots for first visits or by offering assisted scheduling.

#5565. When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide important new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

"There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs."

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies showed that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," said AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

The researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

This discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

The potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," said Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

These substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an important assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically important compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

The first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," said Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy."

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

#5564. Brain implant startup pauses trials

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Annalisa Merelli and O. Rose Broderick

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! Today’s stories have me wondering what it must be like to study the human brain: Every new discovery is a breathtaking revelation, and also a reminder of how little we know, and how far the horizon of full understanding still is. It feels a little like looking at the universe, only what is infinite is, in the most literal sense, ourselves.

For many teenagers, phones are pervasive — and destructive. And the policy proposals and scientific research meant to address the crisis are moving too slowly to help a generation already hooked on screens.

But as STAT’s Isabella Cueto reports, a variety of homegrown initiatives are filling the gap, many of them led by teens. Some programs draw inspiration from Alcoholics Anonymous, helping teens develop tools and strategies to refocus and put their devices away. Others are pushing teens to understand the financial incentives behind holding their attention. The techniques are as varied as they are creative: public interventions, manifestos, and overall a movement that is reclaiming attention, real life connections and, ultimately, freedom. Read all about it here.

Biomarker-based diagnostics have improved our understanding of who may develop severe dementia, advancing our knowledge of Alzheimer’s disease and the hope of finding effective early treatment.

Yet for the people who become aware of their heightened risk, the knowledge is bittersweet. The information allows them to act by taking drugs that may delay dementia onset, but it also carries a weight. In a new First Opinion, Neurotransmissions columnist Jason Karlawish shares how learning of elevated risk changed people’s outlook on the future, from bucket lists to plans for care, to considerations about assisted suicide. (And in case you missed it, check out the first installment in this miniseries here.)

The basal ganglia is a gumball-sized region of the brain so central to psychiatric and neurologic conditions that one scientist called it “the Grand Central station of disease.”

Now a massive scientific collaboration has created a map of the area, including a list of which cells are present and how they arranged. This research has led to the discovery of a new type of neuron, and the identification of cells linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Authors consider it a “monumental achievement” that opens the door for understanding the brain in health and disease, but further progress may be at stake amid government funding cuts, Jonathan Wosen reports.

When STAT’s Megan Molteni started investigating the experimental reproductive procedure known as MRT, or mitochondrial replacement techniques, she didn’t know that she would uncover a sprawling international network of clinics that that market to older women.

Over the course of her reporting, she also found evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking. In fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age.

Read more of her takeaways from this eight-month investigation here. And if you haven’t already read Megan’s original investigation, I encourage you to dig in.

Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation brain-computer interface. The Brooklyn-based startup’s device was a wireless version of its first-generation device, which snakes a catheter through veins to park a stent near the brain’s motor cortex. The aim was to connect users to digital devices using brain activity. The pause is not safety related, leaders said.

It’s the first major hiccup for Synchron, one of the leading companies in a fast-growing industry aimed at helping people with disabilities like ALS and paralysis regain independence through brain implants. Synchron will also eliminate jobs in New York City and is working to develop a new device, WIRED reported.

The news gives context to a cryptic comment CEO Tom Oxley gave on a conference panel in New York City last week. “There are hundreds of components in our system, and it just takes a delayed one to slow down your submission to the FDA,” said Oxley, flanked by his competitors at Neuralink and Precision Neuroscience. “We had one particular component that we were caught up on.” – O. Rose Broderick

Come January, Abdul El-Sayed will be the first epidemiologist in the Senate. His election comes as the U.S. is struggling through a spike in measles cases, a Dengue fever outbreak, and a recent foodborne illness crisis.

STAT’s Nick Florko spoke with the senator-elect about how he hopes to rebuild trust in science, as well as who’s responsible for the current state of affairs. “We didn’t have to get here,” El-Sayed said. “In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information-mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame … our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.” Read the whole meaty interview here.

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this brief. Read below for news from Nov. 2 to 13.

HHS announced a $9.7 million investment Monday through the Administration for Community Living to help prevent elder abuse, neglect and exploitation.

Financial exploitation alone is estimated to cost older Americans $28.3 billion annually, according to the department.

The funding will, among other things, support expanding legal help and strengthening advocacy for those in nursing homes and other care facilities. The ACL will award six new Elder Justice Innovation grants over the next three years, totaling $5.6 million and four new Legal Assistance Enhancement Program grants totaling $1.9 million over two years.

“Older Americans have earned the right to live with dignity, control their own lives, and protect what they worked hard to build,” said Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., HHS secretary, in a statement. “The Trump Administration is investing more than $9.7 million to prevent abuse and financial exploitation, expand access to legal help, and defend the rights of nursing home residents. We are putting practical tools and trusted support into communities to help older Americans safeguard their independence and financial security.”

The Trump administration announced Monday funding for the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), with $10 billion in awards slated for all 50 states.

Similar to fiscal year 2026, Texas and Alaska will receive the largest amount of funding as part of the program. Texas is set to receive $281,976,026, while Alaska will receive $272,653,149.

New Jersey will receive the lowest amount of funding at $142,338,224. Full story.

HHS announced Friday a notice of funding opportunity (NOFO) for its Women’s Initiative for Screening and Health (WISH) program.

The program will award up to $1 million in fiscal year 2027 to establish a multidisciplinary coalition to update HHS’ Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA)-supported Women’s Preventive Services Guidelines.

The funding will fund one organization to create a multidisciplinary panel of at least 10 experts from women’s health, primary care, behavioral health and more. It will also allow the organization to conduct evidence reviews and develop and disseminate information on HRSA guidelines.

“The latest research only makes a difference when it reaches women and the clinicians caring for them,” said Tom Engels, HRSA Administrator, in a statement. “By bringing together clinical expertise and trusted community partners, we can help more women access recommended preventive care nationwide.”

The department says the opportunity advances priorities outlined in an October executive order from President Donald Trump.

CMS plans to trim several “unnecessary” requirements for hospitals and other providers participating in Medicare, including emergency services readiness requirements and staff training for obstetrical services, pushed through during the tail end of the Biden administration.

The proposed rule’s Conditions of Participation (CoP) rollbacks, shared Nov. 5, followed a “comprehensive review” CMS conducted to identify and eliminate “obsolete, outdated and excessively burdensome regulations.” Full story.

CMS finalized its annual outpatient hospital payments rule with a lower-than-proposed rate bump and its major, industry-opposed policy shifts moderated but largely intact.

The 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment Systems rule outlines a 2.3% reimbursement increase for those meeting applicable quality reporting requirements. That’s below the proposed 2.4% increase and reflects a 3.2% projected hospital market basket increase and a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment. Full story.

CMS finalized sweeping Medicare payment reforms it says will shift the program from volume-based "sick care" toward prevention, primary care and accountable care.

The 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule includes a roughly 2% reduction in baseline physician payment rates with targeted increases and new payment opportunities for accountable care, primary and chronic care and behavioral health. Full story.

CMS and HHS announced the finalization of a rule that strengthens oversight of Organ Procurement Organizations (OPO), building on a 2019 Trump executive order.

Key provisions of the final rule include:

“Americans waiting for lifesaving transplants cannot afford poor performance by OPOs, and CMS is committed to holding these organizations accountable,” said Mehmet Oz, M.D., CMS administrator, in a statement. “With today’s new rule, CMS is building on the success of organ procurement reforms from the first Trump Administration to promote clearer documentation, higher donation rates, and swifter consequences for bad actors.”

The Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 25 companies that conduct marketing or generate sales leads for insurers as ACA enrollment season gets underway.

The commission said in an announcement that the letters aim to put these companies on notice about deceptive or unfair marketing tactics that are likely unlawful. Full story.

#5562. Opinion: New organ donation rules are unfair to families

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Tucker is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University.

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.

Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.

Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.

Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.

I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.

The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.

That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.

In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.

These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.

The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.

To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.

Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.

In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.

No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.

I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.

These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.

Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.

First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.

Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.

Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.

The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.

The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.

Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.

In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.

Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

#5561. Omalizumab Linked With Anaphylaxis Elimination in Meat Allergy

— Observational study supports benefit of anti-IgE antibody against alpha-gal syndrome

For patients with alpha-gal syndrome who had severe allergic reactions to red meat despite avoidance, treatment with omalizumab (Xolair) appeared to eliminate anaphylaxis risk in one case series.

Whereas 53% of 64 such patients studied had required epinephrine for a presumed alpha-gal reaction before starting omalizumab, none did while taking the biologic, reported Collette M. Tilly, MD, of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (ACAAI) annual meeting.

All but a few of the patients (95%) reported meaningful improvement in reaction frequency or severity as well, with 33% able to at least partially reintroduce meat into their diet.

"We're definitely encouraged by the results," Tilly told MedPage Today. "Omalizumab is not a cure for alpha-gal syndrome, nor should it be considered [as] putting these patients into remission. But it could reduce reaction frequency and severity, decrease the need for epinephrine, and then potentially even lessen the fear of unexpected reactions. And that would hopefully translate into meaningful improvement in quality of life for these patients."

Omalizumab reduces circulating immunoglobulin E (IgE) available to trigger mast cells that lead to allergic reactions across IgE triggers. Because it's mechanism is not allergen-specific, the antibody is approved to treat IgE-mediated food allergy broadly and has shown induction of tolerance on par with oral immunotherapy.

Alpha-gal syndrome is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to galactose-α-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal) found in beef, pork, lamb, and other meats from mammals as well as animal byproducts such as gelatin. The condition most commonly occurs after tick bites.

"[T]he rationale that specific-IgE is responsible for the reaction and that omalizumab reduces free, and ultimately mast cell bound, IgE provides a logical basis for benefit," Dennis K. Ledford, MD, of the University of South Florida in Tampa, had written earlier this year when a smaller series from the group was reported. "The dose of omalizumab is important, and the treatment does not guarantee ad lib ingestion without adverse events," he added.

Alpha-gal syndrome wasn't included in the randomized trials demonstrating benefit of omalizumab in food allergy. "Milk, egg, peanut, cashew, walnut -- they studied all these foods and that wasn't one of them, obviously," commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis. "But I would still consider that on-label, if you consider alpha-gal a food allergy."

However, alpha-gal syndrome is less predictable than other food allergies, he cautioned. "If you have a peanut allergy, you will react if I perform a challenge; with alpha-gal, it depends on so many things ... It depends on co-factors more often than other food allergies. It depends on the fat content of the food, how much they eat," he said. So a key question is how much meat is allowed to be eaten while on omalizumab, if at all, since the product label notes its use in the context of avoidance, he added.

Use in alpha-gal syndrome has been spreading, although anaphylaxis has been reported in at least one case on patient social media networks. A study of those reported acknowledged potential risk: "Due to omalizumab manufactured in Chinese Hamster Ovary cells, which may variably glycosylate with alpha-gal, the risk of anaphylaxis could be higher."

Tilly's group examined a retrospective, single-center cohort of 64 patients with confirmed alpha-gal syndrome who were treated for at least 3 months with omalizumab from April 2022 through November 2025 and who had at least 3 months of follow-up. The median treatment duration was 23 months, with some patients on the medication for up to 83 months.

Their mean age was 55, and 56% were female. Tilly noted that the cohort was a clinically high-risk population, not a mild, well-controlled one. Among the patients, 81% had documented anaphylaxis reactions to alpha-gal at baseline, and 53% had required epinephrine (34 of 64) before starting omalizumab.

While on omalizumab, 13 of the patients (20%) reported partial reintroduction of mammalian products and eight (13%) had full reintroduction, although physicians continued to recommend avoidance in line with the labeled indications, Tilly said.

Adverse events (AE) while on omalizumab were uncommon, mostly arthralgias, although two patients (3%) discontinued the biologic due to an AE.

Tilly cautioned that the findings could not attribute causation due to lack of an untreated comparator group or prospective outcome assessment. "Symptoms and allergen sensitivity may change over time independent of treatment," she acknowledged.

The study was further limited by potential selection and referral bias as well as the heterogeneous dosing of omalizumab and follow-up duration. Exposure frequency and dose were also not standardized during treatment.

Prospective, multicenter studies are now needed to confirm a treatment effect and to define optimal dosing, treatment duration, and criteria for omalizumab discontinuation, Tilly said.

#5560. Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.

Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.

Coffee Drinkers Showed Much Lower Dementia Rates

One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.

Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health

The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.

Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.

Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.

The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.

How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?

The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.

Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.

Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different

Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.

For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

#5557. Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire

Chutes & Ladders—Mayo Clinic names next CEO; Novant Health CEO to retire" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

>Mayo Clinic has announced Matthew R. Callstrom, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, taking over for Gianrico Farrugia, M.D., who in May announced plans to step down at the end of the year.

Callstrom, a radiologist, has been with Mayo Clinic since 2002 who is currently medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy and its AI Program. He's also a member of its board of governors and board of trustees. He's credited for his role in the major nonprofit system's organizational strategy and integration of AI into care.

Farrugia, who has headed Mayo since 2019, plans to stay on through Dec. 31 to ensure a smooth handoff.

>Carl S. Armato, president and CEO of Winston-Salem, North Carolina-based Novant Health, will retire at the end of this year after 15 years leading the system.

Armato joined the nonprofit in 1998 as vice president of finance and operations in its Charlotte and Winston-Salem physician divisions, and held increasing regional and organization-wide leadership roles over subsequent years.

He's credited with boosting access points and unifying Novant's "collection of strong regional organizations into a unified, innovative health system." He also headed substantial growth, with the organization today counting 45,000 employees, 22 hospitals and about 900 total locations.

With his retirement, current Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer John Gizdic will become president and interim CEO on Jan. 1, 2027. His resume includes over 30 years of healthcare leadership, including more than 20 with Novant.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve."

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find new ways to deliver for our members."

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Company (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the company's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, said her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, company creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her new appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

> Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

Shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC said.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers said in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

Means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick."

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is currently executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo said.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

Parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.

"There are few leaders in healthcare who have the health benefits strategy knowledge and have built the strong relationships that Lisa and James bring to Centivo," said Ashok Subramanian, co-founder and CEO of Centivo, in the announcement. "These new leaders put Centivo in a strong position as we launch in new markets and help more employers across the country tackle rising healthcare costs and restore affordability by rethinking their healthcare benefits strategy."

> Inspira Health CEO Amy Mansue will be retiring at the end of the year, and will be succeeded by current President and Chief Operating Officer Warren Moore, the four-hospital South Jersey system announced this week.

Mansue will have been at the helm for six years, and is credited by the organization for expanding local care access and championing a culture of wellness among its 7,800-person workforce.

Moore has led Inspira's operations since 2021 and was promoted to president at the top of this year. He has 35 years of industry experience and will most immediately prioritize the opening of a new hospital tower and building upon the system's recent Epic launch.

“Leading Inspira has been one of the great privileges of my career,” Mansue said in the announcement. “I’m proud of what our team has accomplished and grateful for the trust of our communities. After working alongside Warren for many years, I know his ability to bring people together, navigate complex challenges and understand what our patients and neighbors count on us to deliver. I have every confidence in his leadership of Inspira’s next chapter.”

> Joint Commission has named Ken Grubbs as its chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1.

Grubbs is the first nurse to serve as COO of Joint Commission Enterprise in organization’s history, according to the Oct. 13 announcement. He currently serves as the organization's chief nursing executive and executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations.

He will succeed James Merlino, M.D., who will take over as the organization's president and CEO this coming January.

> Beth Israel Lahey Health's national leadership search has yielded Peter Shorett as its next president and CEO. His appointment takes effect this coming January.

Shorett is currently the system's senior executive vice president and chief operating officer, and played a role bringing together its Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute for an upcoming strategic collaboration for cancer care. Prior to joining in 2019, he was a senior partner at Chartis.

He'll be taking over for Kevin Tabb, M.D., who in March gave notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year. He'd the role at Beth Israel Deaconess since 2011 and guided the organization through its 2019 merger with Lahey Health.

> WellSpan's Board of Directors has named Laureen Driscoll as the Pennsylvania-based system's new president and CEO.

The executive and registered nurse's appointment will go into effect Jan. 4, 2027. She takes over for Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D., who announced plans to retire this past spring.

Driscoll is joining the 12-hospital, $4.7 billion nonprofit from Providence, where she currently serves as chief executive for its south division and oversees 17 hospitals with $10.3 billion of net operating revenue. Prior to that she held roles at MultiCare Health System, Swedish Health System, Le Bonheur Children's Medical Center and Maine Medical Center.

“She has led complex health systems through transformation while strengthening quality, culture, access and performance," Board Chair Joe Crosswhite said in the announcement. "Just as important, she leads with purpose and understands that listening to team members, clinicians and communities is essential. The Board is confident Laureen is the right leader for WellSpan’s next chapter.”

> UnitedHealthcare has elevated Bobby Hunter to the role of president at the insurer.

Hunter wrote in a LinkedIn post that in the new position he will be tasked with leading the charge on the company's modernization efforts, including investments in technology and other initiatives to simplify the healthcare experience for its members.

Hunter most recently served as CEO of Government Programs at UnitedHealthcare, and has held multiple leadership roles at the insurer dating back to 2011.

"The future we're working toward is one where plans and providers work together more seamlessly, information flows instantly, trust is earned through transparency and accountability, and care teams are able to spend more time focused on patients," he wrote in the post. "To get there, we must continue to deliver on the commitments we make to the people, providers, customers, and communities who count on us every day."

> Jonathan B. Perlin, M.D., Ph.D., will retire from his roles as president and CEO of accrediting organization Joint Commission on Dec. 31. Current Chief Operating Officer James I. Merlino, M.D., is slated to succeed him.

Perlin boasted three decades of healthcare executive leadership across his career, which included five at the top of Joint Commission. During that period he oversaw a substantial reduction on Joint Commission standards deemed to be burdensome or obsolete, and programs to support healthcare safety issues in low- and middle-income countries. Titles preceding his time at the organization included president of clinical operations and chief medical officer for HCA Healthcare, and the U.S. Department of Veteran's Affairs' under secretary for health.

Perlin will remain a strategic advisor to the group following his retirement, holding the title of president emeritus.

Merlino's career included leadership roles at Cleveland Clinic such as chief clinical transformation officer and chief experience officer, as well as at healthcare performance improvement company Press Ganey.

> Robert C. Garrett, CEO of Hackensack Meridian Health, will retire next year after decades with the organization, including its formative 2016 merger.

Garrett is set to step down on June 30, upon which time he'll hold the role of CEO emeritus for a year to help ease the transition. The 18-hospital, nearly $10 billion nonprofit said it plans to announce his successor before the year's end.

Garrett began his career in the early 1980s at Hackensack University Medical Center, and in 2009 was named president and CEO of Hackensack University Health Network. When the organization merged with Meridian Health in 2016 to form New Jersey's largest health system, he served as co-CEO for two years before taking on the solo mantle.

Alongside the organization's growth to more than 500 patient care locations, Garrett's tenure also marked the opening of the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, New Jersey's first new medical school in decades.

"Bob has been the driving force behind HMH's unprecedented growth and transformation, its superior quality, innovation and commitment to building an exceptional workforce," Board Chair Keith Banks said in a statement. "At the heart of Bob's legacy is his unwavering belief that we must deliver the most innovative and compassionate care to all patients. HMH is solidly positioned for continued growth, and we are profoundly grateful to Bob and extend our warmest wishes to him for this well-deserved next chapter."

> The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying group for the pharmacy benefit management industry, has named CVS Health executive Ed DeVaney as its board chair.

DeVaney currently serves as president of CVS Caremark, one of the PBM industry's "Big Three" firms. He succeeds Adam Kautzner, president of Express Scripts and Evernorth Health Services, representing one of the other "Big Three" companies.

“The role PBMs play in lowering costs and improving access to prescription drugs for Americans is critically important,” DeVaney said in the announcement. “As Board Chair, I’m committed to ensuring PCMA shares our story with policymakers, consumers and employers so they have a full understanding of the work we do to fulfill our commitment to lower drug costs.”

> UnitedHealth Group has elevated Dan Kueter to serve as the company's chief commercial officer, per a LinkedIn post.

Kueter previously served as the CEO of UnitedHealthcare's commercial business for four years. UHC is the health insurance arm of UnitedHealth Group.

In the new role, Kueter will be tasked with working across both UnitedHealthcare and Optum to support coordination in product development and innovation, he wrote in the post. He said he will also collaborate closely with other senior leaders at the UnitedHealth Group level.

"I'm looking forward to working across the company with colleagues at Optum and UnitedHealthcare to help drive our next chapter of growth and innovation, focused on helping make healthcare work better for everyone," Kueter wrote.

In a separate post, Brandon Cuevas revealed that he will succeed Kueter as CEO of UHC's commercial unit. Cuevas most recently served as executive vice president for the national health plan at Kaiser Permanente, and he previously held multiple leadership roles during a 14-year stint at UnitedHealthcare.

Cuevas said in the post that he "couldn’t be more excited to rejoin a team that is so capable and committed to making positive change in healthcare."

> Optum has named Ujjwal Ratan as the new chief AI officer for its Optum Insight unit, per a LinkedIn post.

In the role, he will be tasked with leading the development of the critical infrastructure that Optum Insight will build its agentic AI toolset on. Ratan has previously held leadership roles at Amazon Web Services and at Oracle, according to his profile.

"Agentic AI only works if the agents have real, connected data to reason over — and few organizations sit across as much of the healthcare journey as Optum does: providers, payers, pharmacy, life sciences and government programs, under one roof," Ratan wrote. "That's exactly the foundation this next wave of AI needs, and exactly why I think Optum is positioned to set the standard for agentic AI across healthcare, not just inside it."

> Association of American Medical Colleges President and CEO David J. Skorton, M.D., will retire from his post on June 30, 2027, the group announced this week. A search for his replacement is currently under way.

Skorton stepped into the role in July 2019 and was kept on by the board in a unanimous 2023 vote. He's credited with guiding the association through the pandemic and overseeing a comprehensive strategic planning process that brought a new vision and mission.
