#5504. Report: Multiskilling Could Cut Construction Schedules by Up to 38%

A study by the Simplar Foundation found that multiskilled construction crews completed work in approximately 22% to 38% fewer workdays than crews following a traditional single-trade labor strategy. The findings are based on nearly 90,000 labor hours across 18 construction projects involving 11 contractors.

The research, analyzed by Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC), highlights how training workers to perform multiple trades and tasks can help contractors better allocate available labor, reduce downtime, and keep projects moving as workforce demands change.

“America faces a fundamental challenge: We have more to build than our workforce can currently support,” said Michael Bellaman, ABC president and CEO. “This research demonstrates that a solution is already within reach. By investing in our craft professionals, expanding their skills and removing unnecessary barriers to using those skills, we can create more opportunity for workers and greater capacity for contractors to build America.

He continued, “As a new Congress prepares to take office, lawmakers now have powerful evidence to guide policies that strengthen our workforce, promote fair and open competition, and deliver better outcomes for owners and taxpayers. This is an opportunity for the entire construction industry to win.”

Researchers found that relying on single-trade staffing would have left at least one trade short of available labor on 73% of project days. A single-trade approach also required more than one-third additional staffing on the busiest project days.

The study documented 80 unique trade and skill combinations across 18 trades, with multiskilled workers performing an average of 3.2 different trades or skills during their projects.

The findings build on two earlier reports in the foundation’s three-part research series, which found that multiskilling increased the share of workers’ time spent directly advancing construction by 39% and reduced waiting and idle time by 68%. Controlled field trials also showed production rate improvements of 37% to 50%.

The research also emphasizes that productivity gains do not require workers to perform tasks faster or work harder. Instead, allowing properly trained and qualified employees to apply multiple skills can reduce delays between activities, minimize trade handoffs, and improve workflow continuity.

Brian Lines, Ph.D., P.E., the study’s principal investigator and an associate professor at the University of Kansas, said the findings provide measurable evidence of how workforce flexibility can translate into stronger project performance.

ABC is encouraging policymakers to support competency-based workforce development, expand training and upskilling opportunities, and preserve the flexibility of qualified workers to safely perform tasks across multiple skills and trades.

The research was conducted by the Simplar Foundation in collaboration with Arizona State University, the University of Kansas, and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5503. Provo Housing Market: Momentum Meets a Changing Market

As housing conditions shift, a market’s local economy offers an important starting point for understanding where the market is headed. In the Provo, Utah, metro, total nonfarm employment reached 324,000 payrolls in August, up 1.1% from a year earlier, while the unemployment rate declined to 3.4%.

That economic momentum is encouraging, but it is being tested by softer conditions in the housing market.

One important competitive dynamic is the relationship between new and existing home prices. As of July, the median new-home closing price was $495,800, compared with $541,000 for existing homes. That pricing relationship gives builders an avenue to compete with the resale market even as affordability remains challenging.

Sales conditions, however, are mixed. Annualized new-home sales totaled 4,594 units in August, down 6.1% year over year (YOY). Annualized detached sales increased 5.3% YOY, while attached sales declined 17.8%, underscoring different demand conditions by product type.

Supply is another increasingly important part of the story. Finished vacant inventory increased 18.9% YOY to 1,011 units as of Q2 2026. Zonda estimates the Provo market will be 3.89% oversupplied at year-end 2026.

The number of active detached new-home projects decreased roughly 1% YOY as of October while the number of active attached projects was flat. Total building permits are expected to decline by nearly 15% YOY in 2026.

Provo presents a market with two competing realities. Household and employment growth continue to support underlying housing demand, but elevated finished inventory, softer new-home sales, and affordability constraints argue for disciplined production. The projected decline in permitting could eventually help rebalance supply, but near-term execution will remain critical as builders compete for price sensitive buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5502. Homeowner’s Massive 60,000-Light Christmas Display Dubbed a Safety Hazard by HOA

'Tis almost the season for goodwill toward all—unless you’re Neil Heuer and his neighbors.

Heuer, a semiretired tech entrepreneur, lives in Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in community in Waxhaw, NC, with his wife and their children. Over the past several months, he’s been locked in a battle with Aero Plantation's HOA over his annual Halloween and Christmas displays, which his neighbors say disrupt the neighborhood and make them feel unsafe.

Heuer has been putting on the light shows, which include more than 60,000 lights, choreographed animatronic displays, and coordinated music programming, for the past five years. He estimates he's spent more than $70,000 on the exhibitions.

But after last year’s shows, his neighbors began complaining. Those complaints led to a hearing, a lawsuit, and proposed potential changes to the HOA’s bylaws that would prohibit Heuer’s Christmas and Halloween spectaculars in the future.

For his part, Heuer believes the drama has little to do with the lights and more to do with a golf course dispute and a once-anonymous newsletter he penned to bring HOA issues to light.

"I realize that this is a little unorthodox, but, you know, everybody celebrates things differently," Heuer says of his light displays. "I have friends that celebrate their birthday for the entire month and I might be lucky to have a slice of cake on my birthday, but it doesn't matter. This is my hobby. I love to share it with people. I sit outside and record it myself, and I smile. I'm just so giddy with it."It makes me happy, which is good," he continues. "Especially right now, because I do feel like it's draining. It's been a very draining experience."

Six years ago, Neil and his wife, Stephanie, moved to Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in neighborhood with a private airstrip, tennis courts, an equestrian center, and other luxury amenities.

The Heuers' five-bedroom, 8,000-square-foot home sits on 2.36 acres and includes a pool and a four-car garage. Property listing photos show a home hidden in a copse of woods on the edge of a pond.

Heuer tells Realtor.com® he initially got into the holiday displays because of his interest in tech and because his children enjoyed the shows.

“The kids got a kick out of it, and I thought it was cute,” he says.

His neighbors enjoyed the shows, too, he says.“There's a time I can tell you that our neighbors came over and danced in our driveway. We sat and just talked and sat on the front porch and just ... It was really nice," he adds.

Two years ago, though, things took a turn.

Heuer alleges the inciting incident was a disagreement with the HOA board’s vice president over a proposal to “rejuvenate” the community’s golf course. Heuer objected to using reserve funds on the golf course. The vice president offered to pay for the upgrades personally, promising that annual maintenance on the course would be around $8,000, Heuer says.

“After that, I started an anonymous newsletter,” says Heuer. It was meant to “ask questions”

The newsletter "was critical of the HOA, but there was nobody asking these questions. I was anonymous because I really didn't want to receive backlash for asking questions. I didn't want to be on the receiving side of what I'm experiencing now, basically.”

When it was uncovered that Heuer was behind the HOA-critical newsletter, “they basically weaponized the HOA against me,” Heuer says.

At this year’s annual community meeting, when it was revealed that the golf course’s upkeep would run closer to $16,000, he brought up the discrepancy.

“Everybody looked around at me and said, ‘Sit down and shut up,” he says.

Heuer contends that those factors—not the light show itself—have upset his neighbors and led to a hearing earlier this year over alleged HOA violations.

In a letter sent to Heuer in August, the HOA’s legal counsel, Benjamin Karb, wrote that “Inviting unknown members of the public into the subdivision is the type of offensive activity that is a nuisance or annoyance to the neighborhood” and accused Heuer of violating the HOA’s Declaration.

"They believe the roads are private and that nobody belongs here who doesn't live here, I guess," Heuer says. "Let me tell you, 90% of the cars that go by my home I don't recognize. There are people driving by every day who aren't neighbors. And somehow, when they're here to watch my show, they suddenly have a problem. And the people watching my show are families with kids in the backseat."

In September 2026, the HOA held a hearing on the holiday display, alleging it violated the community’s declarations on exterior lighting, signage size, traffic and guest limits, and architectural alterations.

Of major concern was the flow of traffic through the neighborhood by locals looking to see the light show. Aero Plantation is not gated, but it is a private residential community, and the HOA owns and maintains the roads.

In a Sept. 15 letter following the hearing, Karb wrote that when it came to the visitors, the board "did not find a violation exists at this time.”

However, Heuer was found in violation of lighting and signage sizes. The board was unable to make a determination on parking and whether the Heuers had architecturally altered their home’s exterior.

Ironically, the sign that violated the community’s signage limits was one Heuer erected to let visitors know that the off-duty sheriff’s deputies patrolling the neighborhood had been hired by the HOA, not him.

In early October, Heuer filed a lawsuit in North Carolina’s Union Superior Court alleging that the HOA overstepped its authority and failed to provide proper notice and hearing procedures, and that the restrictions being enforced had never been formally adopted in the bylaws.

That case is ongoing, but in the meantime, the HOA board sent out a notice that it was adopting new parking rules in the community.

"While normal visits from family, friends, and personal guests are always welcome, the Rules explicitly address situations where activities conducted, sponsored, or permitted by an Owner attract non-resident traffic—even if the Owner did not personally invite or know each visitor. Owners are held directly responsible for any traffic, stopping, or parking resulting from these activities on our private roads," the notice reads.

Around the same time, a notice was sent to homeowners about two proposed amendments to the bylaws, one of which would establish “standards for public attractions and activities that generate substantial or recurring nonresident traffic within the community.” The other would create “standards for flashing, strobing, pulsating, and high-intensity exterior lighting and authorize the Board to adopt implementing rules consistent with the Declaration.”

The vote on amending the bylaws is scheduled for the end of January, so Heuer plans on going big once more with his holiday display this year.

"Whatever these cockamamie rules that they're trying to change will not apply to this year,” says Heuer.

Realtor.com reached out to the HOA board to inquire about the dispute.

In an emailed response, Aero Plantation HOA President David Arno wrote: “Mr. Heuer filed a lawsuit against the Association, to which the Association will respond through the appropriate legal process. The North Carolina Planned Community Act authorizes an HOA’s members to implement additional changes to a Declaration, which is what members are being asked to decide. The Board does not intend to comment further other than to remind members to voice their opinions by deciding if they want to approve the proposed changes or not.”

After a notice about the proposed amendments were sent out, Heuer emailed his neighbors, imploring them to think twice about adding more amendments to the bylaws.

“Look, you may not like our light show, you may like it. But I don't think we need more rules,” he says.

Regardless of the vote's outcome, Heuer and his wife have decided they’re moving out of Aero Plantation as soon as their youngest daughter, currently a sophomore, graduates from high school.

"There's two things I can assure you," he says. "One is that I will not live here after my daughter graduates. And my next neighborhood will not have an HOA."

She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5499. The Future of Home: 5 Trends for the Next 50 Years

What does the future of housing design look like? Much like with homes today, trends will be tied to how people live. To predict where design is headed, we need to consider how lifestyles are changing, identify which needs have staying power, and anticipate how homes might evolve to meet them.

DAHLIN Group assembled the top trends for the next 50 years to mark the firm’s 50th anniversary, reflecting on decades of design work to determine what the future looks like. According to DAHLIN, these will be key trends:

BUILDER spoke with DAHLIN’s Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, and Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, for their insight on why these trends will endure.

Fifty years is a long time to forecast residential design trends. How did you decide on these five trends, and what’s behind their staying power?

Wagner: A responsible 50-year view should not claim to know the exact layout, style, or construction method people will use. It should identify what future design must be able to do.

The common principle is agency: giving people more useful choices without requiring them to rebuild their lives or surroundings every time circumstances change.

The solutions to these needs will manifest in dramatically different ways over the next 50 years, but the needs themselves are unlikely to disappear.

How will wellness become more integrated?

Julian: Wellness will move deeper into the core decisions that shape everyday performance.

Daylight, window placement and performance, shading, material choices, air filtration, thermal zoning, and access to outdoor space will be considered together, rather than added as isolated features.

We also expect the idea of restorative space to become more distributed. A home does not need one wellness room if daylight, nature, movement, quiet, and thermal comfort are part of the daily path through the house. That makes wellness more relevant across housing types and price points.

The larger shift is from visible elements to a measurable and felt experience: cleaner air, better control, more useful daylight, a stronger relationship to the outdoors, and spaces that support both activity and retreat.

Design is already leaning away from fully open concept. How might this evolve?

Wagner: People want connection without constant exposure. The open plan still serves cooking, gathering, and shared family life extremely well, but a home now has to absorb more simultaneous activities. A call, homework, quiet conversation, and meal preparation may all happen at once.

People do not necessarily want more rooms; they want more control over how rooms relate.

These allow a space to borrow light and belong to the larger home when open, then become visually or acoustically distinct when needed.

Over time, this can make floor plans less defined. A room may shift between office, study, guest space, care space, or retreat because its boundaries and connections were designed to change.

The goal is not maximum openness at every moment. It is to give the homeowner control over when spaces participate in the life of the home and when they recede.

How will the design partnership with AI evolve?

Wagner: AI can already help teams generate and compare more early visual directions, translate abstract language into discussable imagery, and communicate a concept before investing in a complete visualization package. It can also help align a client and design team when they’re using the same word to mean different things.

The important limitation is that human expertise remains vital in framing the challenge, recognizing what is plausible, selecting the direction that serves the client best, and turning an evocative image into architecture that functions.

AI can quickly generate ideas and multiply options, but the designer must still decide which options deserve to move forward and turn them into a workable, real plan.

The near-term model is therefore collaborative. AI broadens the field of possibilities, while human experts frame the question, curate the outputs, and carry the selected idea into a coherent, buildable design.

Homeowners are placing greater importance on opportunities for social connection. How will future site and community planning support this?

Julian: Instead of relying only on a large destination facility such as a clubhouse or pool area, communities can offer a network of smaller lawns, gardens, play and sport areas, outdoor work settings, cafes or neighborhood retail, and places to sit along daily routes.

Smaller scale can also make participation easier and more approachable. It’s easier to join one of a few seats than to become the only person in a room designed for dozens. The same amount of common area can create more opportunities for connection when it’s placed closer to where people live and is shaped for different levels of participation.

When social space is woven into day-to-day patterns, community becomes a series of low-pressure encounters that can grow into familiarity and belonging.

Why will flexibility be the key to longevity in design?

Julian: Flexibility supports longevity when it reduces the cost and disruption of change. A room that has no assigned use may be flexible on paper, but true adaptability comes from practical decisions: useful daylight, appropriate openings, accessible routes, service relationships, and connections to indoor and outdoor space.

Those decisions determine whether a garage bay can credibly become an office or gym, or whether an ADU can serve a renter, a returning child, or an aging parent at different points in time.

The benefit is not that one design and layout lasts forever. It’s designing change into the bones of the home so that the home can adapt for a wide variety of family configurations without becoming obsolete.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

The newlyweds also seemingly have their hands full with a new $5.35. million sprawling lakefront estate in Ohio, not far from Kelce's childhood home. But it's not the only impressive dwelling in the singer's headline-worthy real estate empire.

Over the years, the 14-time Grammy winner has assembled a multimillion-dollar property portfolio that includes eight homes.

The collection spans across New York, Rhode Island, Tennessee, California, Rhode Island, and Ohio, with each home reflecting a different chapter of her life and career.

The singer, who reached superstardom after the release of her 2006 self-titled debut album, has homebuying down to an art.

Let's take a look at some of the properties the Grammy winner has scooped up over the years—from a glamorous landmarked Beverly Hills abode to a downtown Manhattan compound, and more.

Swift grew up on a picturesque Christmas tree farm near Reading, PA, and she honored her childhood home in her 2019 song “Christmas Tree Farm.”

Swift's father, Scott, purchased the 11-acre farm from a client and spent time tending to the grounds when not working his full-time job at Merrill Lynch, according to Refinery29.

A few years later, Swift moved with her family to a nearby house in Wyomissing, PA.

When the property hit the market in 2022, fans got a rare look inside the Georgian-style estate.

Standout features of the five-bedroom house include a sun-drenched breakfast nook, a glossy brick fireplace, and plenty of wainscoting.

The stately residence was listed for $1,099,000 in February and sold for $800,000 in June—a 27% reduction. Is this potential proof that not everything Swift-related turns to gold?

The family moved out of Pennsylvania when Swift was a teen.

In 2003, the family relocated to Hendersonville, TN, so that Swift could pursue a music career. Here, her parents paid $790,000 for a 6,758-square-foot home that sits 30 minutes by car from downtown Nashville.

The waterfront home with "fantastic views" of the Cumberland River features four bedrooms, five bathrooms, and well over an acre. The family still owns the property.

Swift purchased a $2 million luxury condo in Nashville's vibrant Music Row neighborhood for herself just four years after signing a record deal with Big Machine Records.

The three-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom penthouse boasts over 3,500 square feet of living space.

According to reports, she also scooped up the smaller one-bedroom apartment below hers that same year for $387,000. She's still the owner of both units.

Swift added another Tennessee property to her real estate portfolio when she snagged a Greek Revival mansion in the gated Northumberland Estate neighborhood of Nashville.

The singer purchased the four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom mansion in 2011 for $2.5 million. The classic mansion from 1934, which sits on 5 acres, is now estimated to be at least double what she paid.

The glamorous home features a striking curved staircase, vaulted beam ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, and marble fireplaces. Swift purchased the property for her parents.

Swift shook things up in 2012 when she headed West and picked up a $1,775,000 midcentury modern home in Los Angeles.

The four-bedroom abode featured floor-to-ceiling windows, a private courtyard, a lagoon-style pool, and a 1,000-bottle wine cellar.

She sold the property six years later for $2.65 million, clearing nearly a million in profit.

You might have missed this quick flip. In late 2012, Swift bought a seven-bedroom waterfront home in Hyannis Port, MA, for $4.1 million.

The singer sold the property just a few months later for $5.67 million.

If you’re well-versed in Swift’s discography, you're likely familiar with her Watch Hill, RI, retreat. Dubbed “Holiday House,” the historic abode was purchased by Swift for $17.75 million in 2013.

Built in 1930, the extravagant seaside estate once belonged to composer and socialite Rebekah Harkness, who was married to William Hale "Bill" Harkness, “heir to the Standard Oil name and money,” as Swift sings. (Bonus points if you can name the song.)

The mansion features eight bedrooms, a 36-foot-long parlor, and an octagon-shaped dining room.

In 2014, the “Love Story” songstress purchased not one—but two—penthouses in New York City’s ritzy Tribeca neighborhood.

The transaction included a 5,869-square-foot apartment for $14.85 million and a neighboring three-bedroom unit for $5.1 million.

Swift combined the two spaces, creating a massive nine-bedroom, nine-bathroom mega-apartment with wood-beamed ceilings, a dramatic curved staircase, and oversized windows.

She purchased a third unit in the building a few years later for $9.75 million, increasing her New York City home’s layout by over 3,500 square feet.

Swift added a second West Coast abode to her portfolio when she purchased a historic Beverly Hills mansion for $25 million in 2015.

The lovely landmarked estate was once the home of movie producer Samuel Goldwyn, co-founder of Goldwyn Pictures.

Nestled on 2 acres in a cul-de-sac, the nearly 100-year-old home features a championship tennis court, a pool house, and a rose garden.

Despite her dalliances with the West Coast, Swift couldn’t get enough of Tribeca.

In 2017, the musician purchased yet another Tribeca property: the townhome adjacent to her massive penthouse.

The 5,000-square-foot townhouse was transformed into her private penthouse entrance, adding 3,660 square feet to her sprawling city residence. She paid a whopping $18 million for the three-story pad.

Swift famously lived in a sweet Cornelia Street carriage house for part of 2016 and 2017 while her gigantic Tribeca compound underwent renovations.

She rented the circa-1800s four-bedroom, five-bathroom West Village home, complete with blond parquet floors and antique brickwork, for $36,000 a month.

Swift famously immortalized the address in her song "Cornelia Street." It went back up for rent after Swift's departure and is currently off-market.

In 2018, Swift’s father purchased a St. Petersburg, FL, penthouse for $4 million.

Residents of the luxe high-rise have access to 24/7 security, a top-notch fitness center, two heated swimming pools, and a billiards room. Even with the enhanced security, the home was burglarized in 2020.

Although Kelce is the one who snapped up the property, the newlyweds have a gorgeous new place to call home: a palatial eight-bedroom, 8.5-bathroom property the athlete purchased for $5.35 million in March.

The historic residence was built in 1895, and spans an impressive 21,140 square feet. The home was initially listed for $6.99 million in 2024, before the asking price was reduced to $5.99 million the following May.

Kelce secured the estate at a further discount, $1.64 million below its original asking price.

The Bratenahl, OH abode is close to Cleveland Heights, where Kelce grew up alongside his older brother, Jason Kelce.

The proposal had some trouble gaining approval, with a local regulation stating that solid fences and walls—as well as fences with less than 75% openness—cannot exceed 30 inches in height.

However, it seems they've gained quite a bit of support form neighbors, with one speaking anonymously to Page Six to push back on previous reports that the proposal had angered residents.

"I think they're excited," the neighbor told the outlet. "I think it's great. I don't think people are angry."

Randy White contributed research to this report.

#5496. Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

#5495. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.

#5494. Fisher Island Penthouse Sells After $12.2 Million Price Cut—Becoming the Private Island’s Second-Priciest Sale Ever

A stunning seven-bedroom penthouse at Palazzo Della Luna on Fisher Island, which originally hit the market in Miami Beach for $50 million in June 2025, sold on Oct. 28, 2026, for $37.8 million.

Even with a discount of $12.2 million, or about 24%, off its original asking price, the sale is the ultra-exclusive island’s second-highest residential sale ever. The island's top record-breaking sale was a five-bedroom condo that sold for $40 million in 2021.

The seller was represented by Sam Gaita of The Corcoran Group, and the buyer was represented by Andrew Holtz of Compass.

According to The South Florida Business Journal, the seller was “ALJ Properties USA LLC, managed by Alicia L. Jarrett and Camilo Miguel Jr. with the same address in Miami as Mast Capital, where Miguel is founder and CEO.” The penthouse last changed hands for $23.75 million in 2021.

Built in 2019, the sophisticated 9,852-square-foot home has luxurious finishes, including gallery-style walls, wide-oak flooring, and a Boffi kitchen with double Miele and Sub-Zero appliances. The sale works out to $3,837 per square foot.

Floor-to-ceiling windows surround the unit, and retractable glass walls open to 4,500 square feet of outdoor terraces with panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Biscayne Bay, and the Miami skyline.

The lavish primary suite has a fireplace, lounge area, dual walk-in closets, and a fluted marble bath with sweeping 180-degree views.

The condo also has a 2,500-square-foot rooftop terrace for entertaining, with an outdoor kitchen and its own private pool.

“Without question, the private rooftop terrace with a swimming pool is the most impressive feature,” Gaita said. “This is the only ‘lower’ penthouse on Fisher Island offering a private rooftop with a pool, which is an extremely rare feature throughout all of Miami.”

There are also separate staff quarters and garage parking for two cars.

“Fisher Island is an ultra-exclusive, private country club island accessible only by boat or helicopter,” he noted. “This 216-acre private island offers a private beach club, yacht club, multiple dining venues, tennis, pickleball, padel, spa and more, reserved for members and their guests only.”

Gaita said what ultimately drove the record sale was “attracting the buyer who best aligned with and appreciated the one-of-a-kind features the property has to offer.”

He also noted that its exclusive location “on a private island comparable to a country club, isn’t something that can be easily replicated and serious buyers understand that value."

#5493. Google retools Kubernetes for AI agents instead of building a new stack

Agentic workloads are pushing Kubernetes into territory its creators never planned for. Agents generate untrusted code on the fly, sit idle for long stretches and churn through pods at a pace that strains the orchestrator’s control plane.

Cloud providers are now rethinking how general-purpose a cluster should be. Google LLC’s answer is to stop treating every cluster as an infinitely flexible engine and tune each one into a runtime optimized for its workload, according to Jago Macleod (pictured, right), director of engineering for Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine at Google Cloud.

“There isn’t enough memory. There aren’t enough machines. So we have to get more efficient. And so one of the ways that we do that is to focus the Kubernetes cluster on the workload it’s running, and optimize it for that specific workload,” Macleod said.

Macleod and Jaana Dogan (pictured, left), principal engineer at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google is customizing Kubernetes for agentic workloads without fragmenting the open-source ecosystem. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes was built for microservices, then stretched to handle training jobs in which a single pod claims an entire node, Macleod explained. Agents are a different beast again, and some teams have resorted to building custom control planes just to cope.

“I think the agentic workloads are so different in the thrash and the churn that they represent is really not what we built Kubernetes for at all,” Macleod said. “And then agentic applications are almost the polar opposite, which is, you know, in the naive implementation, you just have as many pods as you can possibly fit, and so then the API machinery is running into limits.”

Platform teams have spent a decade making Kubernetes their compute fabric, and customers told Google they did not want agents to fragment it, Dogan explained. Google’s response is Agent Substrate, which runs AI agents in sandboxes directly on Kubernetes. The company donated the project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and recently released version 1.0. Because agents write their own code, that code is untrusted by default and needs sandboxing and network guardrails, according to Dogan. Customers also flagged a costly inefficiency.

“For example, our customers came to us, ‘Hey, majority of the time our agents are idle, but we have to allocate a sandbox all through the lifetime of a session,'” Dogan said. That means wasting a lot of CPU cycles, she explained.

Coding agents are also changing how engineers work, producing more prototypes and smaller, more focused teams, Dogan noted. As agentic workloads multiply, human judgment grows more valuable rather than less, according to Macleod.

“It’s not really, you know, fire off a prompt and forget it and walk away,” Macleod said. “It’s just a different level in the system where you’re applying your judgment and expertise. And that has never been more important.”

(* Disclosure: Google Cloud sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither Google Cloud nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5492. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5491. Bill Cosby Knocks $2 Million Off Original Listing Price of Manhattan Townhouse in Latest Attempt To Sell

Bill Cosby has been looking to offload his longtime New York City townhouse since early 2025, and he's slashed the price once again.

The six-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling now boasts an asking price of $4,999,000, with the listing touting it as a "rare Treadwell Farm townhouse opportunity under $5 million."

The disgraced star first listed the home in April 2025, shortly after news broke that he was facing foreclosure on this property and a much pricier Manhattan townhome he owned at the time.

The more expensive abode was sold for $28 million, while this particular home had a complicated journey.

In July 2025, the asking price was dropped to $6.75 million. Then in December, the listing was removed.

At the time, listing agent Adam Schneider of Corcoran Westside Columbus told Realtor.com® that Cosby and his wife, Camille, chose to delist the home to carry out a series of updates after they resolved the financial issues clouding the property.

"All issues with the lender have been resolved," Schneider said in a December 2025 email. "The property is now being renovated and we plan to list it in the New Year."

The home returned to the market in January 2026 for $6.75 million. At the end of April, the price dipped to $5.99 million.

The townhouse would go on to be listed and removed twice more in 2026—reappearing in August at the same $5.99 million asking, and again in September at a reduced $5.49 million.

The listing directly speaks to the price reduction: "At this reduced price point, the opportunity is clear: there is very little in the 20-foot Upper East Side townhouse market that is this substantial, this flexible, and this well-positioned."

While the listing does not explicitly mention the aforementioned renovation, it does suggest there is still room for change.

"The next owner can preserve what works, improve what matters, and invest directly into a home that reflects their own taste, lifestyle, and long-term vision," it reads.

Spanning 5,000 square feet across a basement and four levels, the property has an open floor plan and includes elevator access and private outdoor space.

"Its flexible floor plan allows for bedroom and bathroom realignment, giving the next owner the option to refresh for the 2020s, personalize, or more fully reimagine the home over time," the listing reads.

The home has a handful of original features, including the red oak banisters, exposed brick, and mahogany and mosaic hardwood flooring.

Crown moldings, high ceilings, and period fireplaces also add character throughout.

A large eat-in kitchen anchors the garden level, and it has been equipped with stainless-steel appliances, including a restaurant-grade Montague Grizzly stove.

A formal dining room includes a wood-burning fireplace, as well as French doors that lead to an enclosed sunroom and a landscaped backyard.

Two generously sized living rooms round out the second level, while the third foor has two large bedrooms and a shared sitting or dressing area.

The primary suite is located on the fourth level and includes a fireplace and two additional spaces that could be used as bedrooms, offices, or other purposes.

The basement includes laundry facilities and storage space, while the rooftop has "meaningful potential for future customization and expansion."

Previous reports indicated that the property had primarily been used by Cosby's son, Ennis, who was murdered in Los Angeles in 1997. It is not clear whether the actor continued to use it regularly, as it is understood that Cosby and his wife—who remained by his side throughout his sexual assault scandal—have been living primarily at their home in a suburb of Philadelphia.

The couple purchased the townhouse in 1980 for $1.19 million.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5489. 4 insights from Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026: AI agents join the team as working colleagues

At Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026, AI agents moved out of single-player chat windows and into shared workspaces. There they work beside people as named, auditable members of the team. Block Inc. built these tools to run itself as an intelligence company, and it is now offering them to other businesses, building on Buzz, its open-source workspace for humans and AI agents. Block introduced Builderlab as a set of tools for teams and AI agents to work together.

The next phase will depend less on how capable a single agent becomes than on how well agents collaborate, share an organization’s context and stay inside firm security boundaries. Block plans to spread that model with open-source code, model-agnostic design and hosted infrastructure. The company is making that push while its core business delivers a third straight guidance raise.

“If you’re talking about making the whole organization more productive, you need to break down these distinctions between what the software does and what the people do,” said Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

Alison Kosik (left) and co-host Gillin spoke with industry experts during Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026 in San Francisco. The interviews covered Block’s open-source business model, agents with their own identities, the shift from prompting to overnight delegation and the security controls that let enterprises trust autonomous systems. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are four standout insights from the event:

Builderlab gives developers endlessly customizable agents on an open-source plug-in architecture, and the launch audience of application builders cheered the idea, according to Gillin. Agents in Buzz have names, avatars and personalities. That shifts the focus from switching among software-as-a-service applications to the work itself, and it could threaten SaaS companies. The revenue model follows the classic open-source pattern of giving the software away and charging for the convenience of a hosted cloud service, he explained. Block said little about commercialization or about Cash App, which brings in 60% of its revenue, according to Gillin.

Most AI tools are built for one person at a time, so each user becomes the bottleneck when results have to be shared with a team, noted Lucas Isaza, product lead of Buzz at Block. In Buzz, agents have their own identities, can be tagged like colleagues and leave an audit trail of every action. Plug-ins, added after the first version launched in July, let anyone reshape the interface. Nontechnical staff, such as account managers building personal dashboards, have been the heaviest users of the companion apps platform. Companies can self-host the open-source code, use a free tier or add funds for remote agents, models and extra storage, Isaza highlighted.

Builderlab sits as an interface layer above the models, so Buzz can use agents from any AI lab and switch to the newest frontier model as it arrives, emphasized Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block. Remote agents run in central cloud environments that are easier to secure than laptops. People can hand them large assignments overnight and act as reviewers. Instead of soft guardrails, agents run on secure building blocks that never grant them permission for certain actions. Some teams have shipped software releases 50% to 75% faster. Axen expects agents to need much less human steering within the next year because they already sit inside the conversation.

Securing agents that act on their own does not mean starting over, because principles such as least privilege, isolated environments and egress controls still apply, shared James Nettesheim, chief information security officer and head of enterprise technology at Block. Builderlab gives every agent a full identity owned by a human, runs it in hardened cloud virtual machines and records its actions in a cryptographically signed ledger that cannot be altered. Block is also building information flow control, which tags data from sensitive sources so the security policy travels with that data and blocks leaks. AI already reviews Block’s code and sorts its security alerts. Nettesheim added that agents let defenders keep pace with attackers’ machine speed.
